title: Albin: Castle Long Behind the Wedge
overview: The Albin's compensation for the gambit pawn is dynamic: the cramping d4-wedge, a lead in development, and an attack. The plan is to trade off White's defenders, castle queenside so the rook lands on the open d-file right behind the wedge, and storm the kingside with the pawns while White is still untangling. Activity and the wedge for the pawn.
pawnBreaks: …f6 or …g5 to open the kingside against the white king
…b5 to pry open the queenside later
pieceManeuvers: …Bxd2 to clear the way for castling
…O-O-O, the king to c8 and rook to the open d-file
strategicThemes: The cramping d4-wedge
Queenside castling, rook behind the wedge
Attacking for the gambit pawn
endgameTransitions: If the attack is parried the d4-wedge can still cramp White into the endgame

annotations: a3 questions the b4-bishop.
…Bxd2+ trades the bishop off, removing a defender and clearing the way to castle.
Qxd2 recaptures.
…O-O-O! the king tucks to c8 and the rook swings to the open d-file, right behind the d4-wedge — rook and pawn pressing deep into White's position.
…Nh6 — developing the knight toward f5 or g4, eyeing the kingside; Black finishes mobilising before striking.
…Nxe5 — regaining the gambit pawn, Black's pieces flooding to active posts with the d4-wedge still cramping White.
…Qxe5 — the queen recaptures on a dominant central square, eyeing the kingside and the open lines toward White's king.
…g5! — the kingside pawn storm begins, the d8-rook already raking the d-file behind the wedge. This is the Albin's dream: pressure on both wings while White is still untangling.

…Ng4 — the knight leaps to g4, spearheading the attack at f2 and h2, the rooks bearing down the g- and d-files. Honest truth: with precise play White keeps the extra pawn and a small edge — but the Albin hands Black a cramping wedge, a lead in development, and a real practical attack for it.
playableLines.title: Albin: Castle Long Behind the Wedge

title: Alekhine: Collect the Chase's Tempi
overview: White wasted moves chasing the knight; Black banks the tempi. The plan: develop with gain of time — …Bb4+, …Nc6, …Bg4 — castle, and surround the weak e5-pawn. Every tempo White spent hunting the knight becomes a Black developing move.
pawnBreaks: keep the e5-pawn weak and fixed
strategicThemes: Punish wasted tempi
Surround the weak e5-pawn
The bishop pair
endgameTransitions: The weak e5-pawn tells in the ending

annotations: Bd2 — White must block the check — another tempo Black banks.
…O-O — Black is already better developed thanks to White's chase.
Bc4 — White develops, but Black already leads in piece activity.
…Nc6 hits the weak e5-pawn; Black surrounds it with the initiative White handed over.
White castles, completing development.
…Bg4 pins the f3-knight — the very piece defending the weak e5-pawn. Black's plan is taking shape: pile onto e5 and the over-extended pawn falls.
White questions the bishop with h3.
…Bxf3! Black trades to remove e5's last defender. The pawn White pushed so eagerly in the Chase Variation becomes a target Black collects — over-extension punished, exactly the Alekhine's promise.
playableLines.title: Alekhine: Collect the Chase's Tempi

title: Alekhine: Active Equality in the Exchange
overview: In the calm Exchange, Black plays for the better-coordinated army. The plan: develop the bishops actively to f5 and f6, pressure d4, and free the position with the …d5 break. White's slight space means nothing against Black's active, harmonious pieces.
strategicThemes: Active piece play vs space
The …d5 break
No weaknesses
endgameTransitions: Balanced, comfortable endings

annotations: Nc3 defends the d4-c4 centre and eyes d5.
…Bg4 pins the f3-knight, leaning on the d4-pawn behind it.
b3 props up the c4-pawn and frees the c1-bishop.
…Bf6 swings onto the long diagonal, doubling the pressure on d4 — Black is fully active and the centre is under siege.
Be3 — White develops and bolsters the d4-pawn.
…d5 — the freeing break, fixing the centre and claiming equal space.
c5 — White grabs queenside space.
…Nc8 — the knight reroutes toward d6 and the blockade.
h3 — White makes luft.
…Be6 — the light bishop takes an active post, eyeing c4 and holding d5; Black has reached comfortable, active equality.
Qd2 — White connects the rooks; the position is balanced.
playableLines.title: Alekhine: Active Equality in the Exchange

title: Alekhine Four Pawns: Dismantle the Big Center
overview: Where the opening leaves off — White has built the Four Pawns center (c4, d4, e5) and Black has provoked it forward exactly to attack it. …f6 strikes the e5-spearhead; once it falls, every black piece is already aimed at the base: Nb6 hits c4, Nc6 and the queen hit d4, the Bb4 pins the defender. The big centre becomes a row of targets.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The engine-backed continuation — Qxf6 is the strong move in this position, carrying out the plan above.

strategicThemes: White’s Four Pawns centre (c4/d4/e5) is overextended — Black provoked it forward precisely to surround and win it.
…f6 strikes the e5-spearhead; when it falls, the d4-base is exposed to the queen, the c6-knight and the rooks.
Every black piece is pre-aimed at the centre: Nb6 hits c4, the Bb4 pins the c3-defender, Bf5 eyes the light squares.

playableLines.title: …f6 collapses the chain, the pieces pile on d4
annotations: exf6 — White grabs the pawn, but the e5-spearhead is gone and Black's pieces all wake at once.
…Qxf6 — the queen recaptures straight onto f6, glaring down the long diagonal at d4 and b2. This is the post the whole plan was built around.
O-O — White hurries the king to safety, but the centre is already cracked open.
…Bxc3 — Black snaps off the c3-knight, fracturing White's queenside pawns and baring the loosened d4-pawn.

title: Alekhine: Undermine the Centre
overview: The Modern Alekhine — Black has provoked White's broad c4/d4/e5 centre and now dismantles it. The plan: pin and trade on f3, pressure e5 with the pieces, and break with …dxe5 and …c5 so the over-extended pawns collapse. Hypermodern chess: let White build, then tear it down.
strategicThemes: Provoke then undermine
The over-extended centre as target
Piece pressure over pawns
endgameTransitions: Once the centre falls Black has the sounder structure

annotations: Nc3 supports the centre.
Black castles, fully developed and ready to undermine.
Be3 props d4 and e5.
…Nc6 adds a piece to the pressure on the d4-pawn and the e5-spearhead — the centre is surrounded.
exd6 — White resolves the centre, removing the e5-spearhead Black was undermining.
…cxd6 — recapturing toward the centre, opening the c-file.
d5 — White gains space and kicks the c6-knight.
…exd5 — Black opens the centre, trading off White’s space advantage.
Nxd5 — White recaptures, centralizing the knight.
…Nxd5 — trading off White’s centralized knight: exactly the Alekhine goal, dissolve the big centre.
Qxd5 — with the centre liquidated and pieces traded, Black has fully equalized.
playableLines.title: Alekhine: Undermine the Centre

title: Alekhine: Simplified Safety
overview: In this Scandinavian-style transposition Black has already neutralised White's centre and equalised material. The plan is calm completion: when c4 kicks the d5-knight it reroutes to f6, the bishops take active posts on d6 and g6, and Black castles into a sound, weakness-free position.
pieceManeuvers: …Nd5-f6 — reroute the knight to a safe square
strategicThemes: Complete development with no weaknesses
Reroute the d5-knight when challenged
Calm, safe equality
endgameTransitions: A symmetrical, healthy structure heads into a level ending

annotations: Nf3 steps the knight back, eyeing the centre.
…e6 opens the f8-bishop and braces d5.
c4 grabs space and puts the question to the d5-knight.
…N5f6 retreats the knight to f6, keeping everything solid.
Nc3 develops, eyeing d5 and e4.
…Bd6 takes the active b8-h2 diagonal.
Nh4 harasses the f5-bishop.
…Bg6 sidesteps, preserving the bishop.
g3 secures the kingside light squares.
…O-O castles; Black is fully developed and without a single weakness.
playableLines.title: Simplified Safety
playableLines.intro: Black reroutes the knight and completes development into a weakness-free position.

title: Alekhine Voronezh: Kingside Play on the Locked Center
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the centre is locked, White’s d5 against Black’s e5. With the middle shut, Black plays on the wing he owns: the kingside. …f5 rolls the pawns forward behind the g7-bishop on the long diagonal, while …c6 can challenge d5 if White over-commits. Classic closed-centre wing strategy.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The kingside break behind the d5-wall — …f5(-f4) gains space and opens lines toward the white king, the natural plan when the centre is locked.
The central challenge — …c6 strikes d5; if White recaptures Black gets play down the c-file and against the loosened centre.

strategicThemes: The centre is LOCKED (White d5 vs Black e5) — Black plays on the wing he controls, the kingside.
…f5(-f4) rolls the kingside pawns forward behind the g7-bishop, opening lines toward the white king.
…c6 is the central counter against d5; the g7-bishop rakes the long diagonal once lines open.

playableLines.title: …f5 — kingside expansion behind the d5-wall
annotations: Be2 — White develops, preparing to challenge the g4-bishop.
…f5 — with the centre locked by d5, Black expands on the kingside.
h3 — White questions the g4-bishop.
…Bxf3 — Black trades, clearing the way for the kingside pawns to roll.

title: Benko Declined: Queenside Files and the …e6 Break
overview: Where the opening leaves off — White declined the gambit with d5, but the Benko’s soul remains: the half-open a- and b-files and a queenside pawn majority. The b6-knight eyes the c4 outpost, the g7-bishop rakes the long diagonal, and the …e6 break opens the centre to convert Black’s pressure into concrete play.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The central break against d5 — …e6 opens the centre and the e-file, turning Black’s queenside pressure into central play.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The b6-knight heads for the c4 outpost — hitting b2 and e3, it cannot be driven off and dominates White’s queenside.

strategicThemes: The half-open a- and b-files plus the queenside majority are Black’s lasting compensation — rooks and queen press a2 and b2.
The b6-knight aims at the c4 outpost; the g7-bishop rakes the long diagonal.
…e6 is the central break that opens lines and converts Black’s pressure into a concrete game.

playableLines.title: …e6 opens the centre
annotations: …e6 — Black strikes at the d5-pawn, opening the centre to feed his queenside pressure.
dxe6 — White grabs the pawn, but this hands Black the open files he was angling for.
…Bxe6 — the bishop develops with tempo; now Black has play in the centre as well as down the a- and b-files.

title: Benko Half-Accepted — activity for the pawn, on schedule
overview: The Half-Accepted tabiya: queen already active on a5, bishop on b7 staring down the long diagonal, and White holding the extra pawn nervously. The plan trades the …e6 lever for open lines the instant White's centre commits — the engine leans White by four-tenths, the Benko's standing rent, and every file that opens pays it down. Activity is the Benko's currency; this line prints it.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The gambit's other break: it forces the d5-centre to declare and opens lines toward the recaptures.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: When the exchanges resolve, the knight lands in the middle of the board with the pawn count improving.

strategicThemes: The Benko pays a pawn for files — open them on schedule or the rent compounds.
…Qa5 and …Bb7 aim before the lines exist; the levers make them real.
Four-tenths down with every piece active is the Benko playing to plan.
endgameTransitions: Benko endings favour Black's queenside pressure even a pawn down — the a- and b-files never close.

annotations: Bd2 — White breaks the a5-e1 pressure at last.
…Qb6 — the queen redeploys, leaning on b2 and the b-file's future.
Qf3 — White centralizes, guarding the long diagonal's traffic.
…e6 — the second lever: the d5-centre must declare itself.
e4 — White props —
…exd5 — we open —
exd5 — and White's pawn returns to d5, now a target instead of a wall.

…Nxd5 — collected. The knight sits in the centre glaring at c3, the material gap narrows to nothing, and the engine's four-tenths for White is the Benko's familiar rent — paid, with every Black piece active and both wing files still to come.
playableLines.title: Activity on Schedule
playableLines.intro: The gambit's second lever opens the centre and the knight collects — rent paid, files open.

title: Benko: The Queenside Squeeze
overview: For the pawn, the Benko buys a lasting positional bind. The fianchettoed g7-bishop rakes the long diagonal into White's queenside, and Black stacks rooks on the half-open a- and b-files behind …Qa5. There's no rush: the pressure on White's queenside IS the compensation, and it only grows.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: Both rooks pile up behind the queenside pawns, on the files the gambit opened.
The queen swings to a5, eyeing the c3-knight and a3 to anchor the squeeze.

strategicThemes: The g7-bishop on the long diagonal
Rooks on the half-open a/b-files
Permanent queenside pressure for the pawn
endgameTransitions: The bind often wins the pawn back with interest as pieces come off

annotations: Nc3 develops; White tries to consolidate the extra pawn behind a calm setup.
…d6 stakes the centre and frees the f8-bishop for its diagonal.
Nf3 develops toward the centre.
…g6 prepares the fianchetto — the Benko bishop heads for the long diagonal.
g3 answers with a fianchetto of its own, contesting that diagonal.
…Bg7 the Benko bishop is home, raking the long diagonal into White's queenside.
Bg2 completes White's kingside development.
…Nbd7 develops, the knight eyeing c5/b6/e5 toward the queenside.
O-O White castles to safety.
…O-O Black castles; now the real work — the queenside files — begins.
Rb1 props b2, bracing for the pressure to come.
…Qa5 swings the queen to the queenside, eyeing the c3-knight and a3 — the squeeze takes shape.
b3 shores up the queenside but leaves a long-term target.
…Rfb8 doubles toward the b-file. With both rooks, the queen, and the g7-bishop trained on White's queenside, Black's pressure is permanent — the Benko's full compensation for the pawn.
playableLines.title: The Benko Queenside Bind
playableLines.intro: Black piles rooks and queen on the a/b-files behind the g7-bishop.

title: Benko Accepted: the Classic File Pressure
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the fully accepted Benko, the purest version of the gambit. Black has the a- and b-files wide open, the g7-bishop on the long diagonal, and a healthy queenside pawn majority. The plan is timeless: …Nbd7, …Qb6 and …Rfb8 pound a2 and b2 while White struggles to untangle.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The central break against d5 — …e6 opens the centre when Black wants to add a second front to the queenside pressure.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The queen lands on b6, joining the rooks on the open files and bearing down on b2 behind the advanced b-pawn.

strategicThemes: The fully open a- and b-files are Black’s gambit pay-off — rooks and queen pile on a2 and b2 for the whole game.
The g7-bishop rakes the long diagonal and the queenside pawn majority is a permanent asset, decisive in the endgame.
White’s knight on b5 is loose; the file pressure forces him into passive defence.

playableLines.title: …Nbd7 and …Qb6 build the queenside pressure
annotations: Re1 — White centralizes the rook.
…Nbd7 — the knight develops toward c5 and e5 and the queenside.
Bf4 — White develops, eyeing d6.
…Qb6 — the queen joins the queenside pressure, eyeing b2 behind the advanced b-pawn.

title: Modern Benoni: the …b5 Queenside Break
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Modern Benoni, where Black’s queenside pawn majority and the g7-bishop are the whole point. Black has just struck with …b5, the thematic break: it opens the a- and b-files, sets the c- and b-pawns rolling, and clears lines for the long-diagonal bishop. Sharp, double-edged, dynamic.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The defining Benoni break — …b5 mobilizes the queenside majority, opens the a- and b-files, and clears the long diagonal for the g7-bishop.

strategicThemes: Black’s queenside pawn majority is the Benoni’s engine — …b5 mobilizes it and opens the a- and b-files for the rooks.
The g7-bishop already rakes the long diagonal at e4; …b5 opens the a- and b-files to feed the attack.
…b5 is often a true pawn sacrifice — Black gives material for the open files, the diagonal and lasting initiative.

playableLines.title: …b5 opens lines, …Bd7 backs the push
annotations: axb5 — White takes, opening the a-file.
…axb5 — Black recaptures; the a-file opens and the queenside majority rolls.
Na5 — White’s knight hops to a5, eyeing the queenside.
…Bd7 — the bishop develops, eyeing the open a-file and backing the queenside push.

title: Bird Classical — the e5 trades and the e7 fork
overview: The Classical Bird resolved into a queenless middlegame with one tactical seam running through it: the e5-pawn's fate. The corpus of the line is a forcing sequence — trade knights on e5, recapture with the f-pawn, and when Black's knight comes hunting the pawn via g4, Nd5 answers with the oldest trick in the open game: the knight takes e5 anyway and Ne7 forks king and c8-bishop. A fifth of a pawn by engine; a whole piece in every blitz game where Black moves fast.

pieceManeuvers.route: c3 → d5 → e7 — the fork route
pieceManeuvers.explanation: The d5 hop looks positional and is tactical: Ne7 forks the castled king and the c8-bishop.

strategicThemes: Queenless is not tactic-less — the e5-pawn is a loaded seam.
Count the defenders of e7 whenever a knight reaches d5 — most opponents don't.
Trade into forcing sequences you have already counted; that is the whole Bird.
endgameTransitions: The f-file and the e5-wedge give White every rook ending — simplify without fear.

annotations: Nxe5 — the trade begins on White's terms.
…Nxe5 — recaptured —
fxe5 — and the f-pawn steps in, opening our rook's file and planting a wedge.
…Ng4 — the knight comes hunting the e5-wedge.
Nd5 — the answer that looks positional and isn't: count what defends e7 now.
…Nxe5 — Black takes the bait pawn —
Ne7+ — the fork: check, and the c8-bishop is attacked in the same breath.
…Kh8 — forced, and the bishop falls next move. A fifth of a pawn at best play — and in fast games, this exact sequence has won a thousand whole pieces. The Bird's tactics live in quiet clothes.
playableLines.title: The e7 Fork
playableLines.intro: Trade on e5, plant the wedge, and let the hungry knight walk into Ne7 — quiet clothes, loaded tactics.

title: Stonewall formation with f4 + d4 + e3 + c3
overview: The Bird can transpose into a Reversed Dutch Stonewall. The plan is to build a permanent kingside pawn wall (f4-d4-e3-c3) and use the dark-squared bishop's mobility for a slow positional grind. Black's …c5 typically forces the c3-pawn into permanent residence, but White's Bf4-g3-h4 maneuver creates kingside attacking chances.

pawnBreaks.explanation: After completing development, g2-g4 opens the kingside for a direct attack. Combined with Rg1 + Qh4 + Bxh7+, this is the Stonewall Bird's main weapon.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The dark-squared bishop reroutes to h4 to pressure Black's kingside and prepare Bxh6 or Bg5 sacrifices.

typicalMistakes: Allowing Black's …f6 break — challenges the Stonewall structure and Black equalizes.
Trading the dark-squared bishop for a knight — gives up the main attacking piece.
strategicThemes: The Stonewall Bird builds an unassailable e5-outpost and a kingside pawn wall, then attacks the black king.
g2-g4-g5 storms the kingside, supported by Rg1 and the queen on h4.
The dark-squared bishop reroutes via f4-g3-h4 to pressure h6 and prepare sacrifices on the black king.

playableLines.title: g4 launches the kingside storm
annotations: h3 — White questions the g4-bishop before launching the storm.
…Bh5 — the bishop retreats along the diagonal.
g4 — the kingside storm begins, gaining space and chasing the bishop.
…Bg6 — the bishop retreats again as White’s pawns roll forward.

title: Bird’s Leningrad: the f-File and Long Diagonal
overview: Where the opening leaves off — a Leningrad-style Bird’s where White’s f4 meets Black’s …e5. Trading on e5 opens the f-file and leaves a cramping pawn on e5, while the g2-bishop rakes the long diagonal — the assets the reversed Dutch is built around. White plays in an open position where his kingside pieces are the more active.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Opens the f-file and leaves a cramping pawn on e5, while the g2-bishop rakes the long diagonal — the reversed-Leningrad break that activates White’s kingside.

strategicThemes: The g2-bishop on the long diagonal and the half-open f-file are the Leningrad Bird’s twin assets.
Trading on e5 opens the f-file and plants a cramping e5-pawn, activating White’s kingside pieces.
White’s f-file pressure and the long light diagonal both aim at the black king.

playableLines.title: Trade on e5, open the f-file
annotations: Nxe5 — White captures, beginning to open lines on the kingside.
…Nxe5 — Black recaptures with the knight.
fxe5 — White recaptures with the pawn; the f-file opens and the e5-pawn cramps Black.
…Ng4 — the knight jumps to g4, hitting the e5-pawn and eyeing f2.

title: Nimzo-Larsen Bird: Central Break and the g-File
overview: Where the opening leaves off — a Bird’s with a Nimzo-Larsen flavour where the dark-squared bishops have been traded off Black’s king. White’s plan is to open the centre with d4, freeing his pieces, while the f4-f5 lever and the half-open g-file (Black recaptured with the king on g7) give play against the slightly airy black king.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The central break — d4 opens the centre and frees White’s pieces, striking at Black’s c5-pawn.
The kingside lever — f5 strikes at g6 and opens lines toward Black’s slightly exposed king on g7.

strategicThemes: With the dark-squared bishops traded, the dark squares around Black’s king on g7 are slightly weak.
d4 opens the centre and frees White’s pieces; f4-f5 pries at the kingside.
The half-open g-file (from …Kxg7) and the f5 lever give White play against the exposed king.

playableLines.title: d4 opens the centre
annotations: d4 — White breaks in the centre, hitting the c5-pawn and freeing his pieces.
…cxd4 — Black trades, but only hands White the open centre he wanted.
exd4 — White recaptures, left with a broad, mobile pawn centre.
…Nf6 — the knight hurries back to blunt that centre and the coming f4-f5 lever.

title: Stonewall Bird — Ne5 and the g-pawn ram
overview: The reversed Stonewall with an extra tempo: the wall stands on c3-d4-e3-f4, and the plan is the structure's eternal one — plant the knight on e5, then march the g-pawn at the kingside while the wall holds everything behind it. The engine calls it dead level; the Stonewall's answer is that level positions with a one-sided attacking plan aren't level on the clock.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The kingside pawn march is the Stonewall's engine; the wall means nothing can counter in the centre.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The e5 outpost is the whole point of the wall — the knight lands and stays.

strategicThemes: A closed centre is a licence for the wing — the Stonewall's founding law.
Plant before you push: Ne5 first, g4 after.
Level engine, one-sided plan: the Stonewall's contract every game.
endgameTransitions: Keep the dark-square bishop pre-trade in mind — the wall's one bad piece decides slow endings.

annotations: Ne5 — the knight takes the post the wall was built to hold.
…Ne7 — Black regroups toward f5.
Nd2 — the other knight props its brother on e5.
…b6 — Black starts the slow queenside answer.
g4 — and the ram begins; the wall behind means no counter-punch exists.
…a5 — the wings race, but only one of them faces a king.
g5 — the ram arrives: the f6-knight must leave its post.
…Ne8 — back it goes. Dead level on the engine, and White's next five moves write themselves while Black's don't — the Stonewall bargain, signed every game.
playableLines.title: Ne5 and the Ram
playableLines.intro: Plant the knight, march the g-pawn — the wall holds while the wing decides.

title: Budapest: Activity Around the e5-Knight
overview: Out of the gambit Black has recouped the pawn and reached the position the Budapest is all about: a strong knight on e5, harmonious pieces, and the initiative. The plan is pure activity — develop the light bishop to f5, swing a rook to the e-file behind the e5-knight, and press White's slightly loose position. The surprise gambit has handed Black an easy, fighting game.

pawnBreaks.explanation: With three attackers on e5, Black recovers the pawn with active pieces.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The knight hops forward to win back the gambit pawn.
The queen adds the decisive third attacker to the gambit pawn.

strategicThemes: The strong e5-knight
Active piece play
Pressing from a surprise gambit
endgameTransitions: The level material and active pieces give a comfortable endgame

annotations: dxe5 — White grabs the gambit pawn, accepting the Budapest's challenge.
…Ng4! The knight leaps forward to attack the e5-pawn, the Budapest's whole point — the pawn cannot be held comfortably.
White defends e5 with Bf4.
…Nc6 develops and adds a second attacker to the e5-pawn.
White develops the knight to f3.
…Bb4+! A check that develops with tempo, forcing White to block awkwardly.
White interposes the knight on d2.
…Qe7! The queen piles onto e5 — three attackers now bear down on the gambit pawn, and Black will regain it with active, harmonious pieces. Ponkratov outplayed Adhiban from this energetic footing.
playableLines.title: The Budapest Gambit (Adhiban–Ponkratov)
playableLines.intro: Black regains the gambit pawn with active pieces.

title: Caro Advance: Counterplay on d4 and the c-file
overview: Black has reached the Caro Advance tabiya after …c5 and …cxd4 cxd4: the c-file is fully open and every black piece converges on White’s d4-pawn — the knight on c6, the queen on b6. White stands a shade better, but Black’s counterplay is concrete and well worth knowing: swarm d4 and contest the open c-file.

pawnBreaks.move: …f6 — the freeing break against the e5-wedge
pawnBreaks.explanation: Undermining the head of White’s pawn chain frees Black’s cramped position and opens the f-file.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The bishop steps off a5 to its best diagonal, safe from a4-a5 and pointing at White’s king.
The knight reroutes toward f5, the strong square in front of White’s pawn chain.

strategicThemes: Pressure the isolated d4-pawn
Own the open c-file
Concrete counterplay against White’s small pull
endgameTransitions: Winning the d4-pawn steers toward an equal or better ending

annotations: White grabs queenside space with a4, harassing the a5-bishop.
…Bc7 reroutes the bishop to the b8-h2 diagonal — safe from a4-a5 and eyeing White's kingside.
White develops the knight toward the f1-g3 regrouping.
…f6! The thematic Advance break: Black strikes the e5-wedge, the pawn that cramps the whole position. Undermine the chain at its head and the game comes alive.
White props up e5 with the rook.
…Nh6 develops the knight headed for f5 — the dream outpost in front of White's pawns.
White reroutes the knight via f1.
…fxe5 opens the f-file for the rook and dissolves White's cramping pawn.
White recaptures, keeping a pawn on e5 for the moment.
…O-O tucks the king away. Black has freed the position with …f6, owns the f-file, and stands comfortably — the Advance's cramp is gone. Carlsen went on to outplay Giri from here.
playableLines.title: The …f6 Break (Giri–Carlsen)
playableLines.intro: Black frees the Advance with the thematic …f6 break.

title: Caro Exchange: Opposite Castling and the …h-Pawn Storm
overview: The Exchange's symmetry hides a sharp plan. With White already castled short, Black develops the bishop to d6 on the b8-h2 diagonal, castles long, and rolls the h-pawn — …h5-h4 — to pry open the h-file against White's king. The h8-rook is already aimed down the file before it even opens.
pieceManeuvers: …Bf8-d6 — the b8-h2 diagonal toward the king
strategicThemes: Opposite-side castling race
Open the h-file with …h5-h4
The …Bd6 diagonal at White's king
endgameTransitions: If the attack stalls the symmetrical pawns hold an easy balance

…h4 strikes at the g3-pawn to rip the h-file open.

hxg3 recaptures; the h-file is now Black's highway.

playableLines.title: Opposite Castling, the …h-Pawn Storm
playableLines.intro: Black castles long and rolls the h-pawn to open the file at White's king.

title: Caro Fantasy: Pressure the Centre, Break with …c5
overview: Against the Fantasy (3.f3), Black castles, develops actively, and turns on White’s broad centre. The rook swings to e8 down the open e-file, the bishop pins from b4, and Black breaks with …c5 to dismantle White’s d4/e-pawn duo. Active, balanced piece play.
strategicThemes: Pressure the broad centre
The open e-file
Break with …c5
endgameTransitions: The freer position favours Black if it simplifies

playableLines.title: Caro Fantasy: Pressure the Centre, Break with …c5

title: Caro Classical: The …c5 Counter-Race
overview: Black has traded the problem light-bishop and built the c6-d5-e6 wall with no weak pieces. White castles long for a kingside storm; Black's answer is the …c5 break, prising open the c-file and the b-file at White's king while the rock-solid structure shrugs off the attack the other way.

pawnBreaks.explanation: After trading the light-squared bishop and developing, …c5 strikes at d4 and opens lines for Black’s counterplay.

playableLines.title: The Classical Plan (Mamedyarov–Topalov)
playableLines.intro: Black develops soundly, trades the bad bishop, and breaks with …c5.

title: Caro Panov: Trade Dark Bishops, Blockade d5
overview: In the Panov, White’s isolated d-pawn (the IQP on d4) is the fight. Black neutralises White’s attacking chances by trading the dark-squared bishops, then plants pieces on the blockade square in front of the pawn and pressures it. A solid, balanced handling of the IQP.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Once the blockade holds and the pieces are placed, …e5 strikes back at the centre and liberates Black’s game.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: One knight blockades the isolani on d5; the other reroutes via e7 to f5/d5 to overprotect it.

pieceManeuvers.route: …Bf6 — pressure d4 on the long diagonal
pieceManeuvers.explanation: The dark-squared bishop adds a third attacker to the isolated d4-pawn.

Blockade and pressure d4
Solid IQP defence

…Nce7 reroutes the knight toward f5 and d5, overprotecting the d5-blockade and adding a defender. This is the anti-IQP masterclass — blockade d5, swarm d4, trade into the ending where the weak pawn falls. Karpov ground Anand down exactly so.
playableLines.title: Playing Against the IQP (Anand–Karpov, 1998)
playableLines.intro: Black blockades and besieges White's isolated queen's pawn.

title: Caro Tartakower — the …c5 file and the regroup
overview: The Tartakower structure deep in its middlegame: doubled f-pawns accepted long ago, both bishops posted, rooks connected behind them. White probes with a3 and c5; the answer is the structure's signature regroup — the bishop drops to b8, the rook slides to c7, and the battery on the b8-h2 diagonal quietly re-aims the whole position. A fifth of a pawn to White on the engine; the Tartakower has held worse for a hundred years.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: When c5 hits the bishop, b8 keeps the diagonal and loads the queen behind it.
The rook's second rank serves both the c-file and the king's defence at once.

strategicThemes: The Tartakower trades pawn shape for the two-bishop stare — keep both aimed.
When a pawn hits your bishop, the retreat that keeps the diagonal is the only retreat.
Regroup behind fixed pawns; they cannot be hurried.
endgameTransitions: The doubled f-pawns hold every minor-piece ending — the structure's old, proven promise.

…Rc7 — the swing floor: the rook serves the c-file and the second rank in one move. A fifth of a pawn to White — the Tartakower's usual rent — with the battery re-aimed and nothing for the probe to bite.
playableLines.title: The Battery Drop
playableLines.intro: c5 hits the bishop; b8 keeps the diagonal — the Tartakower regroup in its natural habitat.

title: Caro Two Knights: Strike with …c5
overview: Pieces have come off and Black sits behind a granite e6-wall with no weaknesses. The plan: complete the fianchetto-free setup and break with …c5, challenging White's centre and freeing every piece for full, easy equality.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Once consolidated with the extra pawn, …e5 strikes the centre and opens lines for Black’s pieces.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The queen holds the extra pawn and offers a trade that defuses White’s gambit pressure.
Black develops and removes White’s best-placed piece, completing a sound setup.

No structural weaknesses
Easy piece play
endgameTransitions: The sound structure equalises smoothly

playableLines.intro: Black consolidates the extra d4-pawn with careful development.

title: Closed Catalan: the e4 Break and Space
overview: Against the solid Closed Catalan, White's whole plan is to engineer the e4-break, activate the g2-bishop, and gain space with e5. The wedge cramps Black and opens a kingside attack.

pawnBreaks.explanation: e4 frees the g2-bishop; e5 gains space and kicks the f6-knight back.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: After the space gain the knight reroutes via e3 toward the f5-outpost and the kingside.

Reroute knights toward f5 for a kingside attack.
endgameTransitions: The space edge and better bishop keep an enduring pull.

title: Open Catalan: Undermine and Recover the Pawn
overview: In the Open Catalan, White does not chase the c4-pawn — he undermines its base with b3, recovers it with interest, and emerges with the bishop pair, the open a-file, and the long-diagonal bishop bearing on the queenside.

pawnBreaks.explanation: b3 strikes the base of the ...b5/c4 chain, dissolving Black's extra pawn on White's terms.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The dark-squared bishop joins its partner on the long diagonal, both bearing toward b7.

strategicThemes: Undermine the c4-pawn with b3 rather than capturing directly.
Recover the pawn with the bishop pair and open lines.
Squeeze with the g2-bishop and pressure down the a- and c-files.
endgameTransitions: The bishop pair and queenside pressure carry into a pleasant endgame.

title: Catalan-Slav — the a-file trade and the long recovery
overview: The Slav-Catalan's grab resolved the Catalan way: Ne5 and the a-file lever already in, and the forced sequence runs the a-rooks off the board with the g2-bishop landing on a8's square — the long diagonal made literal. Dead level says the engine, with the c4-pawn still to be recovered at leisure, which is the Catalan's oldest and favourite job.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The c4-pawn comes home whenever White asks; the asking price is always a better structure.

title: Classical Dutch: the …e5 Freeing Break
overview: Where the opening leaves off — a Classical/Stonewall Dutch where Black has planted the knight on e4 and reached the structure’s holy grail: the …e5 break. Achieving …e5 frees Black’s game in one stroke, opening the centre for the b7-bishop and the rooks and dissolving White’s grip. The e4-knight is the anchor that makes it possible.

…e5 is the freeing break: achieving it opens the centre for the b7-bishop and equalizes in one stroke.

overview: A Classical Dutch where Black combines the kingside …Qe8 reroute with a queenside …b5 break. The plan: attack the king with the queen and f-pawn while expanding and breaking on the queenside with …a5 and …b5 — Black fights across the whole board.

title: Stonewall Dutch: the e4-Knight and the Kingside Storm
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Stonewall, where Black’s d5/e6/f5 pawn wall cedes e5 but builds an unassailable knight on e4 and a kingside attack. With the centre fixed, Black storms: …g5-g4 rolls forward, the f8-rook lifts to h6, and the queen swings to the h-file, all aimed at the white king. The bad c8-bishop is freed via …b6 and …Bb7.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The e4-knight is the Stonewall’s pride — anchored by …f5, it screens the attack and can never be chased by a pawn.

title: Reversed Sicilian: the Queenside Expansion

overview: Black has grabbed a second pawn with ...dxc3. White is two pawns down but enjoys a colossal development lead. The plan is pure attack: Qb3 builds a battery on f7, e5 gains space, and every piece pours toward the king.

playableLines.title: The Evans Declined (Petrosian–Tkachiev)
playableLines.intro: White presses the edge after the gambit is declined.

title: Lasker's Defence: a Small, Sound Edge
overview: Against Lasker's accurate ...Be7, White cannot land a knockout, but by recovering the pawn with a centralised game he keeps a small, pleasant pull — more active pieces and easier development, just as Kasparov showed against Anand.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Building and then resolving the centre lets White regain the pawn with activity.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: After dxe5 the knight centralises on e5, eyeing f7.

strategicThemes: Build the centre with d4.
Recover the pawn with Qa4+ and dxe5.
Keep the more active pieces for a small edge.
endgameTransitions: A pleasant, risk-free pull carries into the endgame.

playableLines.title: Lasker's Defence: a Small, Sound Edge

…Na5 — Black trades off the c4-bishop.

…c6 — Black blocks the check.
White opens the centre with dxe5, the most-played try against Lasker's solid defence — challenging Black's setup before the knight on a5 returns to the game.

…dxe5 recaptures, and the queens come near a trade. Lasker's antidote has neutralised the gambit's fire, but White retains the bishop pair and a small lead in development to press — the principled way to meet the Evans without falling into the attack.

title: Evans Gambit: the e6 Breakthrough
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Evans Gambit in full cry. White gave a pawn for a roaring initiative: the Bc4 and Qb3 train on f7, the Ba3 rakes the dark squares, and the e5-pawn cramps Black. The plan is to strike before Black untangles — e5-e6 pries open f7 and the breakthrough begins.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The engine-backed continuation — Qa4 is the strong move in this position, carrying out the plan above.

strategicThemes: The Evans is a development gambit — White trades a pawn for a roaring lead in development and two raking bishops.
The Bc4/Qb3 battery hammers f7 while the Ba3 rakes the dark squares toward the black king.
Speed is everything — e5-e6 pries open f7 and the attack must land before Black consolidates the extra pawn.

playableLines.title: e6 cracks open f7
annotations: Qa4 — the queen swings to the rim, but from a4 she pins her glare on the offside a5-knight.
…Nxc4 — Black gives up that stranded a5-knight to swap off White's strong c4-bishop and ease the pressure.
Qxc4 — the queen recaptures dead-centre on c4, glaring back down the diagonal at f7.
…Re8 — Black's last piece joins in, the rook lining up on the e-file against White's e5-spearhead.

title: Glek System: the Knight to the f5 Outpost
overview: The Glek's quiet fianchetto setup hides a concrete plan: trade the dark-squared bishops, recapture toward the centre to open the f-file, and reroute the knight via h4 to the f5 outpost. There, supported by the g2-bishop and the f-file rook, White builds a patient but real kingside initiative.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Supported by Re1, the e5 advance opens the long diagonal for the fianchettoed bishop and seizes the centre.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The Glek’s key bishop rakes from g2 toward Black’s queenside and centre.
The rook supports the central advance that opens lines for the bishop.

strategicThemes: Trade the dark-squared bishops, then exploit the dark squares.
Open the f-file with fxe3 for the rook.
Plant a knight on the f5 outpost for a kingside initiative.
endgameTransitions: The space edge and the f5 knight keep a pull even into a queenless middlegame.

…Bb6 retreats the bishop to safety. White has the comfortable Glek setup: the long-diagonal bishop, the half-open b-file, and the e5-break in hand — Mamedyarov outplayed Kramnik from this harmonious position.
playableLines.title: The Glek Fianchetto (Mamedyarov–Kramnik)
playableLines.intro: White fianchettoes and prepares the e5-break.

title: Four Knights Italian: the d4 Break
overview: Where the opening leaves off — a symmetrical Four Knights where the position is balanced but White holds a touch more activity (the e4-bishop, a small space edge). The plan is to open the game on his terms with d3-d4, freeing the bishops and creating the more pleasant middlegame. Patient, but with the initiative.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The central break — d4 strikes e5, opens the centre and frees White’s active bishops for the slightly more pleasant middlegame.

strategicThemes: The structure is near-symmetric and balanced — White’s edge is activity (the e4-bishop) and a touch more space.
d4 is the freeing break: it opens the centre for White’s bishops and creates the more comfortable position.
White plays for a small, lasting initiative rather than a knockout — open the position when his pieces are better placed.

playableLines.title: d4 opens the centre

d4 — White strikes at the e5-pawn — the break that gives this symmetric position life.
…exd4 — Black takes, conceding White the broad centre.
cxd4 — White recaptures, left with a wide pawn centre and the more active bishops.

title: Spanish Four Knights: the Bishop Pair and the d4-d5 Space
overview: The Metger middlegame: White owns the bishop pair after Bxc3 and the doubled c-pawns control extra central squares. The plan is to regroup the bishops, gain space with d4-d5, and slowly open the position where the two bishops outgun Black's bishop and knight.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Once the knight reaches f5, White can break with d4 to open the position for the better-placed pieces.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The reroute toward f5 is the engine of White’s initiative in the Metger.
The Spanish bishop pins and pressures the c6-knight.

strategicThemes: Convert the bishop pair in the increasingly open position.
Gain space with d4-d5 and clamp Black's pieces.
Use the half-open b-file from the doubled c-pawns against the queenside.
endgameTransitions: The two bishops and central space carry into a comfortable endgame edge.

title: Rubinstein: the d4-Break that Unleashes the Bishops
overview: Having met the Rubinstein's …Nd4 with the calm Be2 and traded off Black's active b6-bishop, White holds the bishop pair in a sound position. The c3-pawn was played for one reason: to support the thematic d4-break that opens the centre and turns the two bishops loose.

pawnBreaks.explanation: White expands in the centre to cramp Black and convert the extra pawn.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The knight wins the central pawn, then reroutes to d3 to consolidate.

Prepare and execute the d4-break to open the centre.

title: Scotch Four Knights: Pressure the Isolated Pawn
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Scotch Four Knights with Black saddled by an isolated d5-pawn. White’s whole plan revolves around it: blockade and besiege the isolani, swing a rook to e5, and aim the Bg5 pin plus the Bd3/Qf3 battery at the black king on h7. Pressure on two fronts — the weak pawn and the king.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The engine-backed continuation — Nd1 is the strong move in this position, carrying out the plan above.

strategicThemes: Black’s isolated d5-pawn is the permanent target — White blockades and besieges it.
The Bg5 pin plus the Bd3/Qf3 battery aim at h7; the rook lift Re1-e5-h5 adds the attack.
White presses on two fronts at once — the weak pawn and the black king — and Black struggles to cover both.

playableLines.title: Re5 lifts onto the isolani

title: French Advance: The Queenside Clamp
overview: Against the Advance, Black trades on d4 and then plants a knight on f5 — the dream square that bites at White's d4-pawn, the base of the e5/d4 chain. Behind it Black piles on the half-open c-file with …Rc8 and presses d4 with …Qb6. The plan is slow, structural pressure on the pawn chain's base.

title: French Burn: Queenside Space and the Long Diagonal
overview: In the Burn, Black gives up the centre for free, easy development. The plan is queenside expansion — …a6 and …b5 grab space — and the light-squared bishop swings to b7, raking the long diagonal toward White's king. A comfortable, active setup with no weaknesses.

title: French Classical: The Opposite-Wing Race
overview: White builds the f4/e5 wedge and castles long to storm the kingside; Black answers on the other wing. The plan is …c5 and …b5, blasting open the queenside where White's king will sit. Whoever's pawns arrive first wins — and Black's attack on the castled king is the faster one.

title: French Exchange — symmetry with a job list
overview: The Exchange French's reputation is boredom; its reality is a symmetrical position where the side with the better job list wins. Black's list here: nudge the g5-bishop with …h6, prop with …c6, and post the queen on b6 where it watches b2 and d4 both. When White commits to c4 and c5, the pawn chain declares itself — and every Black piece already stands where the declaration matters. A tenth of a pawn: symmetric material, asymmetric purpose.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The pawn covers d5 today and holds the b6-queen's escape routes forever.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: From b6 the queen leans on b2 and d4 at once — two files of White's queenside expansion answer to her.

strategicThemes: Symmetry is a to-do list, not a verdict — finish yours first.
…h6 before …Qb6: settle the bishop question while the queen's path is clear.

endgameTransitions: Symmetric structures reward the better minor piece in every ending — keep the g4-bishop's trade options open.

title: French Fort Knox: The Impregnable Setup
overview: The Fort Knox solves the French's eternal problem — the bad light-squared bishop — by developing it OUTSIDE the chain to d7-c6, where it trades itself off. What's left is a rock-solid, weakness-free structure with no targets. Black develops calmly and waits; there is simply nothing for White to attack.

title: McCutcheon: Exploit the Wrecked Structure
overview: Black has bartered the dark-squared bishop to cripple White's queenside — doubled c-pawns — and to drag the white king out to d2, where it cannot castle. The plan is to convert those long-term gains: strike d4 with …c5, activate the light-squared bishop via …Bc6, and keep the badly-placed white king under pressure.

title: Milner-Barry: Convert the Extra Pawn
overview: Black accepted the gambit and defended accurately with …Bd7 and …a6, defusing the Nb5 and Bb5+ tricks. Now Black is simply a clean pawn up. …Bb7 — the second bishop joins the long diagonal, doubling the pressure on White’s centre.
d5 — White advances to gain space.
…exd5 opens the centre on Black’s terms.
exd5 — the position opens, and Black’s two bishops and active pieces give full equality.
playableLines.title: Grünfeld: The Long-Diagonal Bishop vs the Centre

intro.say: The Grünfeld’s heart is the g7-bishop on the long diagonal, firing at White’s centre. Black reinforces it with …b6 and …Bb7, keeps the pressure on d4 and e4, and opens the position with …exd5 for the two bishops.
intro.sayShort: Double up on the long diagonal, open with …exd5.

title: Evans Gambit: the Big Centre Attack
overview: The romantic gambit pays for a broad centre and two raking bishops. White rolls d4-d5 to gain space, plants the dark-squared bishop on b2 aimed at g7, and throws the c4-bishop and queen at f7. One pawn for a ferocious attack on the king.

pawnBreaks.move: b4 and d4 — open lines for the initiative
pawnBreaks.explanation: The Evans sacrifices b4 to build the c3-d4 centre and open lines toward the black king.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The bishop bears down on f7, the focus of White’s attack.

pieceManeuvers.route: c3 and d4 — the big centre
pieceManeuvers.explanation: White builds and opens the centre with gain of tempo.

strategicThemes: The gambit pawn buys time to build the d4-e4 centre.
Two bishops on c4 and b2 aim straight at f7 and g7.
White’s open b- and c-files feed the attack while Black’s a5-knight sits offside.
endgameTransitions: If Black survives the attack the extra pawn matters, so White must press while the initiative lasts.

annotations: b4!? The Evans Gambit — White offers a wing pawn to deflect Black's bishop and seize the centre with tempo.
…Bxb4 accepts the challenge, grabbing the pawn.
c3! White hits the bishop, gaining a tempo to prepare the big d4-centre.
…Ba5 retreats, keeping the extra pawn for now.
d4! White slams the centre open, the gambit's whole point — a broad pawn front and open lines for a fistful of tempi.
…exd4 grabs another pawn, but every capture loses time.
White castles, completing development while Black is still untangling — the lead in development is the Evans' compensation.
…Nge7 develops, but White's centre, open lines, and pressure on f7 give a raging initiative for the pawns. Vachier-Lagrave outplayed So from this classic Evans footing.
playableLines.title: The Evans Gambit (Vachier-Lagrave–So)
playableLines.intro: White sacrifices b4 for the centre and the attack.
learnCues: c3 — hit the bishop, gain time

title: Giuoco Piano: the Isolani Initiative
overview: The classical Giuoco Piano middlegame: White accepts an isolated d4-pawn in return for open lines and active pieces. The rook seizes the e-file, the bishop reroutes Bb3-toward f7, and the queen swings to c2 eyeing h7. White hands back the pawn to keep a lasting initiative against the Black king.

pawnBreaks.explanation: When Black is tied to blockading d4, a timely d5 frees the bishop on b3 and opens the centre against the king.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The bishop steps to b3 to stay on the a2-g8 diagonal aimed at f7 after Black harasses it.
The d2-knight jumps into e4, eyeing f6 and d6 and joining the kingside build-up.

strategicThemes: The isolated d4-pawn is a dynamic asset, not a weakness: it grants open lines and active pieces.
White trades the pawn for a sustained initiative; the e-file and the b3-c2 diagonals do the work.
Every minor piece is aimed at f7 and h7 — the Italian target squares.
endgameTransitions: If Black neutralises the initiative, the queenless middlegame still favours White thanks to the freer pieces.

playableLines.title: Giuoco Piano: the Isolani Initiative
annotations: Re1 — the rook seizes the open e-file, pointing down at e8 and the Black king.
…Nb6 — Black nudges the c4-bishop and eyes the d5 and c4 squares.
Bb3 — the bishop slides to b3, staying on the diagonal that aims at f7.
…Nxd4 — Black grabs the isolated d4-pawn, the trade White has been inviting.
Nxd4 — recapturing on d4 with the knight, opening lines toward the king.
…Qxd4 — the queen takes on d4, walking into White’s development.
Qc2 — the queen swings to c2, unveiling the b3-bishop on f7 and loading the b1-h7 diagonal toward h7.
…c6 — Black shores up the d5 and b5 light squares.
Ne4 — the knight leaps to e4, eyeing f6 and d6 as the initiative rolls on.
learnCues: Nb6 — nudge the bishop, eye c4

title: Modern d3: the Nf1-g3-f5 Manoeuvre
overview: The Giuoco Pianissimo plan: White re-routes the queen-knight Nbd2-f1-g3 toward the f5 outpost, recoils the bishop to b3, and prepares the slow d4 break. Patient build-up, then a decisive central strike when every piece is coordinated.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Once the knight reaches g3 and the pieces are coordinated, d4 opens the centre on White’s terms.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The signature modern-Italian re-route: the knight heads for the f5 outpost via f1 and g3.
The bishop recoils to b3 to dodge the trade and keep the a2-g8 diagonal.

strategicThemes: The f5 outpost is the prize — a knight there cannot be chased by a pawn.
White avoids early theory and squeezes from a fully-developed setup.
The d4 break is held back until the pieces are optimally placed.
endgameTransitions: The space edge from a4 and the centre often carries into a pleasant endgame for White.

playableLines.title: Modern d3: the Nf1-g3-f5 Manoeuvre
annotations: …Be6 — Black offers to trade the light-squared bishops on e6.
Bb3 — White declines, sliding the bishop to b3 to keep it on the f7 diagonal.
…h6 — Black takes the g5-square away from White’s pieces.
Nf1 — the knight begins its journey, stepping to f1 on the way to g3.
…Bxb3 — Black trades on b3 to release the tension.
Qxb3 — the queen recaptures on b3, eyeing b7 and the f7-square.
…Re8 — Black centralises the rook on e8 behind the e-pawn.
Ng3 — the knight reaches g3, one leap from the f5 outpost; d4 is next.

title: Møller Attack: the Exchange Sacrifice
overview: The Italian’s sharpest line: after grabbing the rook on a1 Black is invited to drown. White sacrifices the exchange, smashes Bxf7+, and brings every piece to the uncastled king. Pawns and rooks count for nothing next to an attack on a king that cannot run.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The d-pawn joins the assault, opening lines for the f3-queen and the bishops.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The bishop crashes into f7 with check, dragging the king out and ignoring the lost rook.
The knight lands on e5, supporting the f7-bishop and threatening d7 and g6.

strategicThemes: White trades a whole rook for an attack on a king stuck in the centre.
Every White piece attacks; Black’s queenside is asleep and his a1-bishop is marooned.
The attack rolls with checks so Black never gets a move to consolidate.
endgameTransitions: There is no endgame — the Møller is decided in the middlegame by the attack.

playableLines.title: Møller Attack: the Exchange Sacrifice
annotations: …Bxa1 — Black takes the rook on a1, winning the exchange and the bait.
Bxf7+ — the bishop smashes into f7 with check, ignoring the lost rook.
…Kf8 — the king shuffles to f8, stranded in the centre.
Bg5 — the bishop swings to g5 with tempo, harassing the kingside.
…Ne7 — Black props up with the knight on e7.
Ne5 — the knight lands on e5, supporting f7 and eyeing d7 and g6.
…Bxd4 — Black grabs the d4-pawn, but the attack is already decisive.
Bg6 — the bishop sacrifices again on g6 to rip open the king; the hurricane rolls on.
learnCues: Bg6 — sacrifice again, rip the king

title: Two Knights with d4: the Forcing Sequence
overview: The dynamic d4 line: White gambits a pawn for a development lead, pins the e4-knight on the e-file, and uses the Bxd5/Nc3 fork to regain material. Precise play leads to a balanced middlegame where White’s rook and structure give a small, lasting pull.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The early d4 surrenders a pawn to open lines toward Black’s uncastled king.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The c3-knight forks the queen on d5 and the e4-knight, regaining the piece.
The e1-rook lands on e6 deep in Black’s camp after the knights trade.

strategicThemes: A development lead is the compensation for the gambit pawn.
The pin on the e-file is the engine of every White threat.
After the smoke clears White has the better structure and the active rook.
endgameTransitions: The resulting near-endgame is level material but White’s active rook on e6 presses Black’s weaknesses.

playableLines.title: Two Knights with d4: the Forcing Sequence
annotations: …Qa5 — the queen flees the c3-fork to a5.
Nxe4 — White scoops the e4-knight back, restoring material equality.
…Be6 — Black covers f7 and develops the bishop to e6.
Neg5 — the knight hops to g5, attacking the e6-bishop and f7 again.
…O-O-O — Black castles long out of the pin.
Nxe6 — White trades on e6 to damage Black’s structure.
…fxe6 — recapturing on e6 leaves Black with a weak e-pawn.
Rxe6 — the rook grabs e6, landing actively in Black’s position.
…Bd6 — Black develops the bishop to d6 and the dust settles, White slightly better.
learnCues: O-O-O — castle out of the pin

title: Bb3 bishop, c4-d4 centre, Nc3-d5 clamp (Modern main line)
overview: In the Modern main line White hands the gambit pawn back and converts to a positional bind: the c4-bishop reroutes to b3, c4 and d4 build a broad centre, the knight swings via c3 to d5, and Bxf4 recovers the pawn with a dominant, open game and a lasting initiative.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The central pawn push that opens lines for both rooks and the queen. Once d4 fires, the Bc1 develops with tempo (Bxf4 or via e3-Be3), and the Nf3 has the e5 square as an outpost.
When Black has played …Nf6, e4-e5 kicks the knight and clears the e-file for the Re1 + Qe2 battery.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: Qe2 prepares Nc3 (otherwise pinned), supports d4 + e5 pushes, and aligns on the e-file behind a future Re1. The queen swings to h5 or g4 later for direct kingside attack.

typicalMistakes: Pushing g4 too early to defend f4 — weakens the king and lets Black counterattack with …Qh4+ ideas.
Trading on f4 with the bishop without sufficient piece development — gives Black time to consolidate.

playableLines.title: Convert the gambit into a central bind
annotations: …Be6 offers to trade White’s strong bishop and shields f7.
Bb3 sidesteps the trade, keeping the bishop on the long diagonal eyeing the knight on d5.
…Be7 develops the bishop to e7, completing Black’s kingside.
c4 gains space and kicks the knight on d5 back to b6.
…Nb6 retreats the knight to b6.
d4 erects the broad c4-d4 centre — the heart of White’s plan.
…Nxc4 grabs the c4-pawn.
Nc3 develops and heads for d5.
…Nb6 steps back from the c4 skirmish.
d5 clamps the centre and shuts the light-squared bishop out.
…Bg4 pins along the d1-h5 line.
Bxf4 recovers the gambit pawn, the bishop sweeping the c1-h6 diagonal toward h6.
learnCues: Be6 — offer the trade, shield f7
c4 — gain space, kick the knight
d5 — clamp, shut out the bishop
Bg4 — pin on the d1-h5 line

title: Open f-file pressure after fxe5
overview: The opening sacrifice of the f-pawn fully opens the f-file once O-O lands. The Rf1 immediately pressures f7 with the Bc4. Combined with Qe2 or Qd3 and a follow-up h2-h3 + Kh1 to safely store the king, White builds a heavy attack against Black's underdeveloped kingside.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Pushing h2-h4 attacks Black's g5 pawn shield (after Black's …g5 holding the f4-pawn). The pawn storm on the h-file opens lines toward Black's king before Black can complete development.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The dark-squared bishop develops to defend the kingside and prepare queen-rook coordination. Be3 supports the central d4 pawn; Bd2 prepares Nc3 + 0-0-0 to attack on opposite wings.
The c3-knight aims for d5, the most active outpost in the King's Gambit. From d5 the knight pressures Black's queenside and threatens to land on f6 or e7 with a tempo-gaining sacrifice.

typicalMistakes: Forgetting to capture f4 early — Black can consolidate the extra pawn into a fortress if White delays.
Castling kingside without enough cover — once Kg1, the open f-file cuts both ways.

playableLines.title: The g3 lever: undermine the f4-g5 chain and open the f-file
annotations: …h6 props the g5-pawn so the f4-g5 chain holds firm.
c3 braces the d4-pawn and frees c2 for the bishop, preparing the g3 break.
…Nc6 develops, pressing the d4-pawn.
g3 strikes the base of the f4-g5 chain — the lever that pries the f-file open.
…Bh3 forks the rook on f1, the critical counter.
gxf4 dissolves the chain and rips the f-file open.
…Bxf1 grabs the exchange on f1.
Qxf1 recaptures; for the exchange White owns the open f-file and the bare squares around f7.
…gxf4 wins the pawn back, but every White piece now swarms the f-file toward f7.
learnCues: g3 — the lever on the chain

title: KIA vs the mirror — Nc4, the pin trade, dead level
overview: The full symmetric King's Indian — both sides fianchettoed, both castled, the a-pawns already locked. The plan is the mirror-breaker's checklist: the queen's knight to c4 where it leans on e5, the rook behind the e-pawn, and when …Bg4 pins, trade on f6 rather than suffer — handing Black doubled pawns' worth of structure for the bishop pair's worth of nothing in a symmetric position. Dead level, says the engine; the checklist says who's more comfortable.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The KIA knight's home in every structure: from c4 it presses e5 and d6 forever.

pieceManeuvers.route: c1 → g5 × f6 — the pin resolved forward
pieceManeuvers.explanation: Rather than suffer …Bg4, White sets the same pin and trades it off on his own clock.

strategicThemes: In mirrors, the first useful asymmetry wins — Nc4 is it.
Answer a pin threat by setting your own first.
Bishop-for-knight into doubled pawns is fine when the structure stays closed.
endgameTransitions: The locked a4-a5 pawns hand White the b5 square in every ending — the mirror's one lasting gift.

annotations: Nc4 — the family square: the knight leans on e5 and d6 both.
…Re8 — Black backs the stake.
Re1 — mirrored, as everything here is —
…Be6 — Black offers the c4-knight a question.
Bg5 — answered with a bigger one: the pin lands on f6 first.
…h6 — the nudge.
Bxf6 — and we resolve it forward: bishop for knight, on our clock.

…Qxf6 — the recapture keeps Black whole. Dead level on the engine — a mirror at peace — and White's remaining pieces all know their squares while Black's still hold their breath. That's the KIA's version of an edge.
playableLines.title: The Mirror-Breaker's Checklist
playableLines.intro: Nc4 first, the pin set and resolved forward — small asymmetries in a position at peace.

title: KIA vs French: the e5-Wedge Kingside Attack
overview: The archetypal KIA: clamp the centre with the e5-wedge, reroute the knight Nf1-h2-g4, and storm the kingside with h4-g4-g5 while Black plays on the other wing. White's attack at the king usually arrives first.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The e5-wedge cramps Black and frees White's hands for the kingside assault.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The signature KIA reroute, bringing the knight to g4 for the kingside attack.

strategicThemes: Clamp the centre with the e5-wedge.
Reroute Nf1-h2-g4 toward the king.
Storm with h4-g4-g5; win the opposite-wing race.
endgameTransitions: If the attack is parried, the e5-space keeps White comfortable.

…Ba6 — offering to trade the light bishops to ease Black's cramped position.

title: King’s Indian Mar del Plata: the Kingside Storm
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Mar del Plata King’s Indian, the sharpest opposite-wing race in chess. The centre is locked (White d5/c5 vs Black e5/f4), so both sides attack: White rolls the c-file on the queenside, Black storms the white king. …g5-g4 cracks open f3, the rooks and knights pour to the kingside, and the f4-pawn freezes White’s defenders.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The storm’s hammer — …g5-g4 strikes f3 and tears open the kingside; after fxg4 the knight and rooks pour through toward the white king.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The f6-knight leaps to g4, into the heart of the attack, hitting f2 and h2 around the white king.

strategicThemes: The centre is LOCKED — so it is a pure race: White attacks the queenside with c5, Black storms the kingside. Speed is everything.
…g5-g4 strikes f3 to crack open lines at the white king; the f4-pawn freezes White’s e2-bishop and g-pawn.
Black throws everything kingside — …Nf6-g4, the rook lift …Rf8-f6-g6/h6, and …Qe8-h5 join the assault.

playableLines.title: …h5 prepares, …g4 cracks the king
annotations: Rc1 — White readies the queenside break with c5.
…h5 — Black prepares the storm, supporting the …g4 advance.
a4 — White pushes on the queenside, the other wing of the race.
…g4! — the kingside storm strikes f3, prying open lines at the white king.

title: Jobava: the Kingside Lunge and the e5 Outpost
overview: The Jobava's whole appeal is a London structure carrying a genuine attack. Lunge with h4 to gain kingside space, reroute the knight to the e5-outpost, and lift a rook to the third rank — the quiet London turned aggressive.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The h4-h5 lunge cracks open the kingside in front of Black's castled king.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: After h4, the rook lifts to h3 and swings along the third rank toward the kingside.

strategicThemes: Use the early Nc3 for an aggressive, fast set-up.
Lunge with h4 to gain kingside space.
Plant a knight on e5 and lift a rook to attack.
endgameTransitions: If the attack is parried, the e5-knight and space still favour White.

title: London vs KID: c4 Central Expansion
overview: Where the opening leaves off — a London System against a King’s Indian setup, where White has a solid d4/c3 centre and the harmonious London pieces. The plan is to expand with c4, claiming central and queenside space, while the knight eyes the e5 outpost and the dark-squared bishop and queen probe the kingside. Solid, then expanding.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The engine-backed continuation — Qd1 is the strong move in this position, carrying out the plan above.

strategicThemes: White’s d4/c3 centre is solid and harmonious — the London pieces all have natural, active squares.
c4 expands in the centre and on the queenside, claiming space and preparing d5.
The knight eyes the e5 outpost; the dark-squared bishop and queen probe the kingside dark squares.

c4 — White expands, claiming central and queenside space and challenging the d5-bishop at once.

title: London System: The e5-Outpost and f4 Kingside Play
overview: The London's whole point is the e5-outpost. Once Black develops with …b6 and …Bb7, White plants a knight on e5 — unchallenged by any black pawn — braces it with f2-f4, and swings the queen to f3 toward the kingside. With the bishop on g3 and the knight on e5, White has a genuine slow-burn attacking scheme on the kingside.

title: Nimzo 4.f3: Clamp and Exploit
overview: White's 4.f3 over-reached for a big centre and got doubled c-pawns instead. Black has clamped the queenside with …c4. The plan: develop the pieces against the static weaknesses, target the doubled c-pawns and the c4-clamp's cramping effect, and exploit White's slow, committal play.

title: Nimzo (…d5): Two Bishops and the …c5 Break
overview: Where the opening leaves off — a symmetric d5-vs-d4 center where Black kept both bishops, aimed at the white king (Bd6 and Bb7). Black has just struck the queenside with …a5; the plan is to undermine White’s b-pawn (…a5, …c6) while preparing the …c5 break to open the center for the two bishops. A kingside knight jump to e4 adds the second front.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The freeing central break, striking d4 to open lines for the b7- and d6-bishops aimed at White’s king.
When White locks with b5, …c6 undermines the b-pawn and opens queenside lines for Black’s rooks.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The knight jumps to e4, the central outpost, joining the two bishops’ pressure toward the white king.

strategicThemes: Black owns the two bishops, aimed at the white king (Bd6 on the b8-h2 diagonal, Bb7 on the long light diagonal) — the …c5 break opens the position for them.
On the queenside Black undermines White’s pawns with …a5 and …c6, opening files for the rooks.
A knight jump to e4 plants a piece in White’s camp and reinforces the kingside attack the two bishops promise.

title: Nimzo Hübner: Blockade the Doubled Pawns
overview: The Hübner — Black has doubled White's c-pawns with …Bxc3 and clamped the centre with …d6/…e5. The plan is pure Nimzowitsch: blockade the doubled c-pawns on the light squares, dominate with the knights, and besiege the fixed weakness while White's bishops sit blunted by the locked pawns.

title: Nimzo Kasparov: Grind the Doubled Pawns
overview: Where the opening leaves off — Black has traded on c3 and left White with a doubled, isolated c-pawn. The plan is positional and patient: reroute the knight Nd5-b6-c4 to the dream outpost, trade queens into an endgame where the weakness tells, and let the a6-bishop rake the long light diagonal. Black presses a near-symmetric balance toward a win.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Black’s one central lever — …e5 (once prepared) gains space and frees the e6-pawn; otherwise the plan is pure piece pressure on the weak c3-pawn, not a pawn break.

overview: The centre is bolted shut — Black’s d6-e5 against White’s c4-d5 — so the game shifts to the wings. With no central counterplay available to White, Black expands on the kingside: …g5 and …Nh5 gain space and target White’s king, while the king tucks toward the queenside. Black is comfortable, even a shade better.

title: Nimzo Rubinstein — the d5 crisis, mapped
overview: The Rubinstein Nimzo at its one tactical crisis: White has pushed d5 and our bishop has taken on c3, and for four moves everything hangs at once. The map through: the pawns and bishops trade on e6 and f3 in forced order, White regains his piece with the b-pawn recapture, and the smoke clears at seven-tenths for White — the Nimzo's price in this exact line, stated plainly. What the number buys Black: the bishop-pair imbalance is gone, the structure is fixed, and the position plays itself while White's wrecked kingside pawns don't.

endgameTransitions: White's doubled f-pawns are the permanent feature — every ending collects against them.

title: Nimzo Saemisch: Blockade the Doubled Pawns, Break with …f5
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Saemisch, where Black gave up the dark-squared bishop to saddle White with doubled, isolated c-pawns (c3 and c4). That structure is Black’s whole game: blockade the pawns, attack c4 with …Na5 and …Ba6, and challenge White’s broad e4/f4 center with …f5. Keep the queenside fixed — never …cxd4, which would let White undouble.

title: Old Indian: Knight Outpost and the …f5 Break
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Old Indian, a solid cousin of the King’s Indian with the centre locked by d5 against e5. Black’s plan is patient wing play: the knight sits on the c5 outpost hitting e4, the knight reroutes off f6 to free the …f5 break, and …a5-a4 gains queenside space. Quiet, manoeuvring, then a break.

The plan is pure positional pressure: route the a5-knight to the c4 outpost, clamp the queenside with …b5, and grind the weak pawns. Equalise first, then outplay.

overview: Black has reached the Improved Hanham ideal and just played the freeing break …d5. The cramped, solid Philidor structure now bursts open in Black's favour: the b7-bishop comes alive, the rooks find open files, and the Hanham knight on d7 springs to its dream square in the centre. The plan is to trade into a free, active middlegame where every black piece outworks its counterpart.

title: 150 Attack: Trade the Bishop, Win the Race
overview: The 150 Attack is a blunt, dangerous plan: Be3, Qd2, f3, then Bh6 to trade off Black's great dark-squared defender, castle queenside, and storm the h-pawn at Black's king. Black's antidote is speed on the other wing. The key is the early ...c6, launching ...b5-b4 and freeing the queen. When White trades on h6, Black accepts the slightly airier king and immediately strikes back with ...Qa5 — the queen leaps into the game, eyes the c3-knight, and lends weight to the queenside pawn storm. Whoever's storm lands first wins; Black must not flinch and must not slow down.

title: Pirc Austrian — the race, collected
overview: Twenty-five moves of the Austrian race distilled to its collection point: Black's queenside pawns have marched to b5 and c4, the b8-rook stands loaded, and White's kingside gestures have spent themselves. The finish is the race's payoff — when White's rook lifts looking for one more attack, the knights cash the e4-pawn with a double capture the engine grades at plus one point four for BLACK. The Austrian gives Black this race every game; this is what winning it looks like.

From a cramped, passive-looking start Black reaches a position with active pieces and no weaknesses — exactly what the Classical Pirc promises.

When the centre finally resolves with dxe5 dxe5, Black has a sound, harmonious position with no weaknesses — exactly what the Czech promises.

overview: The Advance tabiya with the good bishop already out on f5 — the whole point of the Caro move order. The engine reads a whisker for White at the end — the Caro's standing tax, paid in exchange for a position with no losing plans in it.

title: vs the Fantasy — grab, give back, untangle
overview: Honesty first: facing the Fantasy from the Black side costs — the engine leans White by nearly nine-tenths in this line, and the narration will not pretend otherwise. The plan is the survival kit: bank the d4-pawn, meet the Bb3 retreat with …Be6 offering the trade that unloads the pressure, and when e5 kicks the knight, the …Bd5 block holds the light squares together. A hard line played with open eyes — the alternative is not knowing, and that costs more.

title: Najdorf main — the …b5 race and the Nd5 storm
overview: The Bg5 main line at full boil: White castled long, our queen sits on c7, and the race is the whole game. The plan is the Najdorf's oldest religion — …b5, …Bb7, …b4 rolling at the king while White's pieces mass in the centre. When the thematic Nd5 sacrifice lands, taking is both forced and best: the engine holds Black together at a sixth of a pawn in the wreckage. Both sides all in; the prepared player cashes.

title: Main line — the c4 bind against the hedgehog
overview: The check on b5 bought the tempi, the bishop tucked home through d3 to f1, and the pawn already stands on c4: the bind is built. His corpus rides this exact structure — thirteen games continue right here — and the plan is patient occupation: rebuild the centre with d4, recapture with the knight, reinforce with b3, and let Black's hedgehog run out of safe pawn moves.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The central rebuild: d4 converts the bind into space — after the trade the knight recaptures and sits on the best square in the position.
The quiet cement: b3 ties c4 and the long diagonal together so the bind can never be chipped by ...b5.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The d4-recapture is the bind's centrepiece — from d4 the knight watches b5, c6 and e6 while the c4/e4 pawns fence everything else.

strategicThemes: The Maróczy squeeze: space without weaknesses — Black must create the first target.
His thirteen-game continuation: Be7, d4, O-O, b3 — every developing move also cements the bind.
endgameTransitions: The well-placed pieces hold the edge into the endgame.

annotations: Black completes the kingside — the hedgehog shell of a6, b6, d6 and e6 is finished. Shells hold until the space runs out.

Black takes — declining just leaves White a full centre plus the file.
The knight recaptures and the bind is complete: pawns on c4 and e4, the knight on d4 watching b5, c6 and e6 at once.
Black castles into the shell. Nothing is wrong with Black's position except the future: every break needs White's permission.
And b3, the quiet star — c4 is cemented, the c1-bishop gets the long diagonal, and the squeeze plays itself. His games score this structure heavily.

title: Berlin Endgame: Majority vs the Bishop Pair
overview: The Berlin's queenless middlegame is one of the most important structures in modern chess — Kramnik used it to dethrone Kasparov. The queens are off and Black's king has lost castling, but Black owns the bishop pair and a structure that will not crack. White's only winning try is to convert the clean kingside pawn majority into a passed pawn; Black blockades on f5, walks the king to safety, contests the open d-file, and aims to prove the majority can never advance. It is decided square by square, not by force.

pawnBreaks.explanation: White's central winning idea: roll the kingside majority. Black's ...h5 is the standard antidote, freezing g4 and securing the f5-outpost.
A slower majority advance, gaining space and challenging the blockading knight — but it concedes squares and must be timed carefully.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The Berlin king is a fighting piece — it walks to e8 and onward, sheltering on the kingside and supporting the pawns in the endgame.
Black's knight on f5 is the soul of the defence: it blockades the kingside majority and cannot easily be dislodged once ...h5 is in.
The bishop pair fans out to the long diagonals, the source of Black's counterplay and the reason the majority is so hard to push.

strategicThemes: White's only structural trump is the clean four-vs-three kingside majority that can one day make a passed pawn; the entire game is whether it can ever safely advance.
Black's bishop pair and the f5-knight blockade are the counterweight — long diagonals plus a frozen majority usually add up to a fortress at the top level.
The open d-file is the main artery: whoever controls it dictates where the heavy pieces operate.
Black's doubled c-pawns are the long-term weakness White probes, but they also shield the king and control central squares.
endgameTransitions: This IS the endgame — the Berlin reaches a queenless middlegame by move sixteen, so technique is everything from the start.
If White trades into a pure pawn ending the majority can win, so Black keeps minor pieces on to leverage the bishops against the structure.
