Black unbundles; the dark-squared bishop frees the king and connects the rooks.
White seizes the open d-file, the natural artery for pressure in this endgame.
Black's bishop reaches e6, activating the bishop pair and shoring up the light squares.
playableLines.title: The Queenless Middlegame
learnCues: Be7 — free the king, connect rooks

title: The Berlin Endgame
overview: After the queens come off on move eight, the Berlin becomes a queenless middlegame that has frustrated the strongest players alive. Black holds the bishop pair but a king stuck in the centre and doubled c-pawns; White owns the e5-pawn, a healthy kingside majority, and the safer structure. Watch the tabiya arise, then learn to press it — patiently, the way Kramnik did against Kasparov.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Buttress and expand the e5-pawn and the kingside majority.
Gain space and challenge the well-placed knight when the time is right.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: Reroute the queen-knight to reinforce e5 and eye the d6 and f6 holes.
Seize the open d-file with check, harassing Black's uncastled king.

strategicThemes: White's trumps are the e5-pawn, the kingside majority, and Black's stranded king — not material.
Restrain the bishop pair by keeping the position half-closed; open it only when your structure tells.
Patience: the Berlin is pressed (or held) over forty quiet moves, not won by a knockout.
endgameTransitions: Black's bishop pair fights White's structure — the kingside majority is the long-term winning try.
Fix and blockade the doubled c-pawns and White's healthy majority becomes the decisive factor.

annotations: The Berlin Defence — Black ignores the bishop and hits e4.
White castles and offers the pawn.
Black takes it: the Open Berlin.
White strikes the centre rather than chase the pawn back.
The knight drops back to hit the bishop and douse White's initiative.
The same structural blow as the Exchange — White doubles Black's c-pawns.
The knight heads for d4 or e3.
The queens come off with check —

— and Black recaptures with the king, losing the right to castle. This is the Berlin endgame: Black has the bishop pair, but White owns the e5-pawn, a healthy kingside majority, and the safer king. A queenless grind where White presses for the long haul.
playableLines.title: The Queenless Wall

title: Breyer: Wing Play on the Closed Center
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Breyer tabiya, the center locked by White’s d5 against Black’s e5. With the center shut, the game is decided on the wings. White’s lever is b3, striking the c4-pawn Black left behind when he closed the queenside; the b-file opens and b5 becomes a target. On the other wing the g3-knight eyes f5, and the Bc2 sits on the b1-h7 diagonal. Patient maneuvering, then a wing break.

pawnBreaks.explanation: White’s main lever. b3 hits the c4-pawn Black pushed past; after …cxb3 Bxb3 the b-file is half-open and Black’s b5-pawn becomes a lasting target on the queenside.
The kingside alternative. When Black commits to the queenside, f4 strikes e5 and opens the f-file toward the black king — sharper, played when White wants the attack rather than the squeeze.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The g3-knight jumps to f5 — the kingside outpost. If …gxf5 then exf5 rips open the g-file and the Bc2 diagonal toward the black king.

strategicThemes: The center is LOCKED (White d5 vs Black e5) — so the game is fought on the wings, exactly as Capablanca taught: with the centre closed, attack where you have the space.
b3 is the key lever: it undermines Black’s over-extended c4-pawn, half-opens the b-file, and leaves b5 weak for White’s rooks and bishop to target.
On the kingside the g3-knight heads for the f5 outpost and the Bc2 trains on the b1-h7 diagonal — the second front White can switch to if the queenside stalls.

playableLines.title: b3 — cracking the queenside on a closed center
annotations: Black challenges the pin with …h6, asking the g5-bishop to declare itself.
Be3 — the bishop steps back but keeps eyeing c5 and the queenside dark squares.
…Bg7 — Black completes the fianchetto, the bishop joining the long diagonal.
b3! — White strikes at the c4-pawn, the weakness Black left when he locked the queenside. Lines begin to open.
…cxb3 — Black gives up c4; the b-file half-opens.
…Bxb3 — the bishop recaptures on the a2-g8 diagonal. White has the half-open b-file and a lasting target on b5.
learnCues: …Bxb3 — target b5 on the half-open file

title: Breyer: From Reroute to Endgame
overview: The Breyer is patience with a destination. Black's knight retreats all the way home to reroute through d7; White completes a harmonious build-up and — crucially — tucks the bishop to c2. Watch the structure lock, then understand where it's headed: a two-winged battle whose endgame favours White's kingside space.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Lock the centre with d5, then expand on the kingside with f4 — the space that wins the ending.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The Breyer reroute — home and back out to d7, propping e5 and freeing the b7-bishop.
Prophylaxis: off b3 so Noah's Ark can never spring, and onto the b1-h7 diagonal for the kingside.

strategicThemes: Bc2 makes the Noah's Ark trap structurally impossible — the maneuver IS the defence.
Two-winged play: White presses the kingside (f5, the space), Black the queenside.
The endgame is the Breyer's pay-off — White's space and the f5-outpost convert when the pieces come off.
endgameTransitions: Trade into a heavy-piece or minor-piece ending and White's kingside space and the f5-square become decisive.
Black's queenside majority is the counter-trump; whoever's structure is sounder when the queens vanish wins.

annotations: The Breyer's calling card — the knight retreats all the way home, to reroute through d7 and free the b7-bishop's long diagonal.

And the quiet move that does double duty: Bc2. It develops toward the kingside AND tucks the bishop safely off b3 — sidestepping the Noah's Ark trap forever. The cage Black dreams of can never close. That single piece of prophylaxis is the whole reason the closed main lines retreat this bishop.

Black grabs queenside space and the centre locks. Now look past the middlegame: trade the heavy pieces and White's kingside space plus the f5-square are the trumps that decide the ending. The Breyer is patience that cashes out in the endgame.
playableLines.title: The Reroute, the Prophylaxis, the Plan
learnCues: c5 — lock the centre; space tells

title: Chigorin: Wing Play on the Closed Center
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Chigorin Ruy with the center locked, White’s d5 against Black’s e5. With the middle shut, both sides play on the wings. White’s main asset is the f5 outpost: the f1-knight reroutes via g3 to f5, the square Black can never chase with a pawn. The available pawn breaks are b4, hitting Black’s c5, and the prepared f4 (after the f3-knight steps aside) to open the kingside.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The queenside lever. b4 strikes Black’s c5-pawn; after …cxb4 cxb4 the c-file opens for White’s rooks — the immediately available break while the kingside knight maneuvers.
The kingside break, prepared by stepping the f3-knight aside (Nh2). f4 hits e5 and opens the f-file toward the black king when White commits to the attack.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The signature closed-Ruy reroute. The knight steers to f5 — the outpost Black cannot chase with a pawn — pressing d6, h6 and the kingside.

strategicThemes: The center is LOCKED (White d5 vs Black e5) — so play shifts to the wings, the way Capablanca taught: with the centre closed, expand where you hold the space.
White’s main asset is the f5 outpost: the f1-knight reroutes via g3, and from f5 it presses d6 and h6 and screens a kingside attack.
The pawn breaks are b4 against Black’s c5 (queenside) and the prepared f4 (kingside); Black’s own counter is …f5, so White must judge which wing to open first.

playableLines.title: Nf1-g3 toward f5, then the b4 wing break
annotations: …Ne8 — Black reroutes the knight toward g7 and f5 to blunt White’s kingside.
Ng3 — the knight heads for the f5 outpost behind the locked center.
…g6 — Black takes the f5-square away from the knight.
b4! — with the kingside walled off by …g6, White switches wings, striking c5 to open the queenside.

title: Chigorin: Queenside Space into the Ending
overview: For decades the Chigorin WAS the main line. Black's ...Na5 hits the Spanish bishop, ...c5 claims queenside space, and White retreats to c2 — both answering the knight and dodging the Noah's Ark trap. The knight tours to e3 hunting d5/f5. Where it's all heading: a queenside-minority versus central-space ending.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Build the centre and clamp with d5, fixing the structure for the two-winged ending.
Probe the queenside to fix Black's majority before the endgame.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: Hits the b3-bishop — the Chigorin's defining idea (and the reason White must retreat it).
Answers ...Na5 and dodges Noah's Ark in one — the maneuver is the trap's antidote.
The long tour to e3, hunting the d5 and f5 outposts.

strategicThemes: Bc2 is forced AND prophylactic — it parries ...Na5 and erases the Noah's Ark trap together.
Black's queenside minority versus White's central space — that imbalance carries into the ending.
The d5/f5 outposts are the prize; owning them in the endgame usually decides it.
endgameTransitions: A queenside-minority-vs-central-space ending: White's space and outposts tell as pieces come off.
If Black's minority attack stalls, White's healthier centre converts the endgame.

annotations: The Chigorin's signature — ...Na5 jumps at the b3-bishop and demands it move.
Bc2 — and it is not merely a retreat. It answers the knight AND tucks the bishop off b3, so the Noah's Ark trap can never spring. Prophylaxis and development in a single move.
The knight completes its tour to e3, eyeing the d5- and f5-outposts — the squares the whole middlegame revolves around.

Black blunts the knight with g6. Now the shape of the ending is set: Black's queenside minority pawns press, White's central space and the d5/f5 squares answer. Trade down and that space is the deciding word.
playableLines.title: The Knight Hits, the Bishop Hides, the Space Tells
learnCues: g6 — blunt the knight; space tells

title: Closed Ruy after d4 — the h6 trade and the a-file clock
overview: The full Closed Ruy — Breyer shape, fianchetto answer, the d4-e5 tension humming. The plan is the modern handling: trade the dark-square bishops through h6 the moment Black's lands on g7, then start the a-file clock with Rad1 waiting behind it. The engine gives four-tenths — the Closed Ruy's compound interest — and the position keeps every promise the opening ever makes: more space, more time, more plans.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The g7-bishop is the king's best defender; h6 removes it at the cost of nothing.

pieceManeuvers.route: d1 → d2 → h6 — into the hole
pieceManeuvers.explanation: The queen follows the trade into the dark-square hole it created.

strategicThemes: Trade the fianchetto bishop and the dark squares change owners forever.
The Ruy's edge is compound interest — collect it in tempi, not tactics.
Every Black regroup answers our last move; none advance his own plan.
endgameTransitions: The space edge converts through every simplification — the Ruy's four-tenths never expires.

annotations: Qd2 — the queen steps behind the coming trade.
…Qe7 — Black connects.
Bh6 — the offer the g7-bishop cannot decline —
…Bxh6 — taken —
Qxh6 — and the queen sits in the hole the trade created, eyeing the dark squares around the king.
…a5 — Black seeks the wing.
Rad1 — the last piece joins; the d-file waits behind the tension.
…c5 — and Black finally stakes his claim at d4. Four-tenths on the engine — the Closed Ruy's compound interest, collected as always: more space, more time, and a queen already through the door.
playableLines.title: The h6 Trade
playableLines.intro: Remove the king's best defender, follow with the queen — the Ruy's compound interest, collected.

title: Exchange Ruy: The Structural Endgame
overview: Fischer's favourite way to play the Ruy: White trades on c6 on purpose, surrendering the bishop pair to inflict doubled c-pawns. The result is a clean four-vs-three kingside majority that can make a passed pawn, against a black queenside crippled by the doubled pawns that never can. White steers toward an endgame — even inviting the queens off — and grinds. Black's compensation is real: the two bishops and a broad pawn centre give active middlegame play. The fight is a race between Black's bishops and White's superior structure.

pawnBreaks.explanation: White's winning plan is to mobilize the healthy kingside majority; f3 supports e4 and prepares the pawn storm that can manufacture a passed pawn.
Black gains central space and frees the bishops, using the doubled c-pawns dynamically before they become a static endgame weakness.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: White retreats the knight to b3, sidestepping ...c5 and steering toward the endgame where the pure structure decides.
Black's light-squared bishop is the most active piece — it pressures f3 from g4, then reroutes to e6 to hold the light squares and probe the queenside.
In the queenless endgame the white king marches to the centre to support the kingside majority and add a piece to the advance.

strategicThemes: White's entire game rests on one fact: a clean kingside majority that can make a passed pawn versus a black queenside crippled by doubled c-pawns that cannot.
Black's compensation is the bishop pair and a broad centre — dynamic factors that must tell before the board empties and structure dominates.
White happily trades pieces and even queens to reach the ending where the structural edge is decisive; Black avoids mass exchanges to keep the bishops biting.
It is the photographic negative of the Marshall — no sacrifice, no attack, just the accumulation and conversion of one small, lasting advantage.
endgameTransitions: The Exchange aims directly at the endgame: trade down, march the kingside majority, make a passed pawn, win. This is the structure's whole purpose.
If Black activates the bishops and opens the position before White consolidates, the bishop pair can hold or even seize the initiative — so White trades patiently.

annotations: Black grabs central space and prevents White's knight from settling, leaning on the bishop pair.
White retreats the knight, content to head for an endgame where his structure tells.
Black invites the queen trade; even queenless, the bishops give real activity.
White recaptures with the rook, taking the open d-file into the endgame.
Black's bishop swings to g4, raking the back rank and pressuring f3.
White challenges the bishop and prepares to advance the kingside majority — the whole point of the Exchange.
Black's bishop reroutes to e6, holding the light squares and eyeing White's queenside.
White completes development; the long technical fight begins — majority versus the two bishops.
playableLines.title: Majority vs Bishops
learnCues: c5 — space, lean on the bishops
Bg4 — rake the back rank, hit f3

title: Endgame: The Kingside Majority
overview: The Exchange isn't really about the opening — it's about the ending. By trading on c6 and doubling Black's c-pawns, White earns a healthy kingside pawn majority that manufactures a passed pawn, while Black's crippled queenside makes nothing. Watch the structure form, then play it out — this is Fischer's whole reason for the line.

pawnBreaks.move: f4 / g4 / h4 — the kingside roll
pawnBreaks.explanation: Advance the healthy kingside majority to manufacture the passed pawn.
The central thrust that fixes the structure and frees the majority to roll.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: In a king-and-pawn ending the king is a fighting piece — march it up to escort the passer.

strategicThemes: White's kingside 4-v-3 makes a passer; Black's doubled c-pawns make none — that single asymmetry is the whole game.
Trade pieces, not pawns: every exchange drags the position toward the winning king-and-pawn ending.
Black's compensation is the bishop pair and activity — keep things closed enough that structure outweighs it.
endgameTransitions: The pure king-and-pawn ending is winning for White: the kingside majority queens a pawn while Black's queenside cannot.
Even with one pair of rooks left on, the outside passed pawn tends to decide in White's favour.

annotations: The Spanish bishop eyes c6 — the knight that holds e5 in place.
Black pokes the bishop: the Morphy move.
The Exchange. White gives up the bishop pair on purpose — the point is structural, and it lasts all the way into the endgame.
The forced recapture doubles Black's c-pawns: four queenside pawns on three files. They can never make a passed pawn.
Black shores up e5.
White challenges the centre, steering toward the trade that defines the ending.

Now read the pawns. White's kingside — e, f, g, h — is a clean four against three: that majority makes a passed pawn. Black's extra pawn is the doubled c, and it makes nothing. Trade every piece and White wins the king-and-pawn ending. This is why Fischer played the Exchange.
playableLines.title: Fischer's Structural Endgame

title: Ruy Lopez: Meet f4 by Liquidating the Centre
overview: When White lashes out with an early f4 in the Ruy, Black does not panic — Black takes (…exf4), strikes in the centre with …d5, and liquidates. After the central pawns and queens come off, Black reaches a comfortable, equal ending with no weaknesses, White’s aggression having achieved nothing.
pieceManeuvers: trade queens into a safe ending
strategicThemes: Liquidate White’s f4 aggression
Central break with …d5
Simplify to a sound ending
endgameTransitions: If the middlegame attack doesn't decide things, White's active rooks on the open f-file and potentially the e-file give lasting endgame activity. Active rooks on open files always outperform passive defenders.

The Ruy Lopez f4 plan often leads to positions where White retains the bishop pair after exchanging on f4. In an open endgame with the f-file available, two bishops combined with rook activity create a decisive advantage.

annotations: …exf4 accepts — opening lines that favour the better-developed side.
d3 props the centre.
…d5! the central counter-strike.
Bxf4
…dxe4 liquidates the centre.
dxe4
…Na5 redeploys, eyeing c4.
Qxd8
…Rxd8 — queens off, and Black has a comfortable, equal ending. White’s f4 lunge gained nothing.
playableLines.title: Ruy Lopez: Meet f4 by Liquidating the Centre

intro.say: Against an early f4, Black doesn’t panic: take with …exf4, strike with …d5, and liquidate the centre. Queens come off and Black reaches a sound, equal ending — White’s aggression spent for nothing.

title: Marshall Attack: A Pawn for the Initiative
overview: The Marshall is the great exception to the Ruy Lopez's patience. Black sacrifices the e5-pawn with ...d5 to blow the centre open and pour every piece at White's king. White is a clean pawn up and must defend with absolute precision: the queen swings to h3, the bishop to d6, the rooks to the e-file, and a single inaccuracy is fatal. The plan for Black is not to regain the pawn but to keep a permanent, paralysing initiative; the plan for White is to return the pawn at the right moment, blunt the attack with g3 and Be3-Qd3, and emerge a pawn up in a calmer position.

pawnBreaks.explanation: White's d4 returns part of the gambit material to free the position and blunt Black's piece pressure, blocking the d6-bishop's diagonal toward h2.
Black's thematic lever to open lines and activate the b7-bishop and rooks against White's centre once the attack is rolling.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The signature Marshall queen lift. From h3 the queen pins White to the defence of g2 and the light squares around the king, the focal point of the whole attack.
Both bishops swing to the kingside — d6 toward h2, g4 raking the back rank — so every minor piece points at White's king.
A rook drops onto the e-file behind the action, adding a heavy piece to the attack and contesting the only open file.

strategicThemes: Black's compensation is the initiative, not the pawn — every piece reaches an attacking post before White can untangle, and the threat of ...Qh3 with mating ideas around g2 is permanent.
White's defensive plan is concrete: g3 to stop the immediate mate, Be3 and Qd3 to return the pawn and trade attackers, then consolidate a pawn up.
The light squares around White's king (g2, f3, h3) are the battleground; once g3 is played they become permanent holes Black's pieces target.
Practical danger outweighs the engine evaluation — White must find a string of only-moves, which is why so many strong players avoid the Marshall with the Anti-Marshall a4.
endgameTransitions: If White survives the attack and trades the heavy pieces, the extra pawn decides — the Marshall is all-or-nothing for Black, with little to fall back on if the initiative fizzles.
When Black regains the pawn but enters an endgame, the bishop pair and active rooks usually hold the balance rather than win, so Black keeps queens on to press.

annotations: White returns part of the structure with tempo, but the pawn count still favours him — the real story is Black's coming initiative.
Black aims the bishop at the kingside, joining the attack with tempo against h2.
White's rook steps back to e1 to defend the back ranks against the gathering storm.
The queen leaps to h4 — the classic Marshall lift — threatening to land on h3 beside White's king.
White blunts the immediate mating ideas with g3, accepting a permanent light-square weakening.
The queen settles on h3, glued to White's king and eyeing g2 — the heart of the attack.
White develops with tempo and prepares Qd3, returning the pawn for coordinated defence.
Black's last piece joins in; the bishop on g4 rakes the back rank and ties White down.
White centralizes the queen to defend g3 and contest the light squares — the Marshall's bargain is struck.
playableLines.title: The Attack Crashes In
learnCues: d4 — return a pawn with tempo
g3 — blunt mate, weaken light squares

title: Open Ruy: Piece Activity vs the Light Squares
overview: The Open Variation is the Ruy turned inside out: instead of the patient main line, Black grabs e4 and plays for fast piece activity and a race. The defining structure is Black's d5-pawn screened by the e6-bishop, anchoring an active knight. White leans on the b3-bishop's pressure against e6 and the loose light squares to prove the pawn-grab was premature, often trading on e6 to open the f-file in front of Black's king. The battle is Black's activity against White's concrete targets.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Black's thematic space-grab: the d4-pawn cramps White and grants a protected outpost, the backbone of Black's active setup.
White undermines the d4-pawn and fights for the central dark squares before Black can entrench.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The e4-knight retreats to its ideal square c5, hitting the b3-bishop and supporting Black's queenside and centre.
White's light-squared bishop is the star: from b3 it pressures e6 and f7, often combining with Ng5 to trade off Black's defender of the light squares.
White develops the queen-knight toward the kingside, eyeing the g5-jump that wins the e6-bishop and cracks open the f-file.

strategicThemes: Black plays for activity and a race, not material — every piece reaches an aggressive post quickly, and the d4-pawn cramps White.
White targets the light squares around e6 and f7 that Black's setup leaves loose, especially once the e6-bishop is traded.
Opening the f-file in front of Black's often-uncastled king is a recurring White theme after Nxe6 fxe6.
The imbalance is permanent: Black's piece activity and centre against White's structural targets — whoever's trumps speak first wins.
endgameTransitions: If the pieces come off, Black's broken e6/e-pawns and light-square holes become a lasting endgame liability for Black.
When Black keeps the initiative alive, the active knight on c5 and the d4-pawn can carry the middlegame before structure matters.

annotations: White reroutes the knight toward the kingside and prepares to challenge Black's active pieces.
Black's knight swings to c5, hitting the b3-bishop and eyeing the e4 and d3 squares.
White bolsters the centre and clamps the d4-square before Black can use it.
Black grabs space with d4, gaining a protected outpost and cramping White.
White's knight jumps to g5 to trade off Black's prized e6-bishop, guardian of the light squares.
Black grabs the c3-pawn, accepting open lines in return — the Open Ruy's permanent imbalance.
White trades on e6, eliminating the strong bishop and exposing Black's king.
Black recaptures, opening the f-file but accepting weak, isolated e-pawns — activity against structure.
playableLines.title: Activity Meets the Targets

title: Open Ruy: Activity into the Ending
overview: The Open Ruy is the antithesis of the closed manoeuvring lines — Black takes on e4 and the game opens at once. The structure that results, Black's mobile d5-pawn against White's e5 wedge, carries straight into a piece-activity endgame: not patience, but coordination.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Open the centre with d4, then challenge d5 with c4 to clarify the structure for the ending.
Support and expand the e5-wedge to cramp Black before trading down.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: Reroute to b3, eyeing c5 and d4 and contesting the light squares.
The Spanish bishop keeps the a2-g8 diagonal — a long-term trump into the ending.

strategicThemes: The Open is activity, not patience — the better-coordinated army wins the ending.
Black's mobile d5-pawn vs White's e5-wedge is the defining imbalance, all the way down.
The bishop pair and open lines favour White if the position stays sharp into the endgame.
endgameTransitions: An open, piece-active ending: White's bishop pair and the e5-wedge tell if coordination holds.
If Black's d5-pawn becomes weak rather than mobile, White's pressure converts the endgame.

annotations: The Open Ruy — Black grabs the e4-pawn instead of defending it. The position cracks open; this is the most active, least patient way to meet the Spanish.
White strikes the centre back at once — in the Open, the open lines are worth far more than a pawn.
Black props the knight with d5, claiming the centre and the e6-square for the bishop. Here is the structure that defines the Open: Black's mobile d5-pawn against White's e5 wedge.
Nbd2 — the knight reroutes to b3 to bear down on c5 and the d5/c5 light squares.
playableLines.title: The Open Structure into the Ending
learnCues: d5 — prop the knight, claim space

title: Zaitsev: The Rook Lift Attack
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Zaitsev with White’s d5 locking the center and the rook already lifting via a3. The signature plan is the Ra1-a3-g3 swing: the rook joins a kingside attack the closed center makes safe. Black locks the queenside with …c4 (or counters with …f5); White clears f3 with Nh2, completes the lift to g3, and storms with g4.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The engine-backed break — axb5 is the principled continuation here, gaining ground in the structure the plan describes.

strategicThemes: The center is LOCKED by d5 — so White attacks the king on the kingside, the closed centre guaranteeing his own king’s safety while he commits forces.
The Ra1-a3-g3 rook lift is the signature: the rook reaches g3 the long way round to spearhead the attack, after Nh2 clears the third rank.
Black answers with …c4 (locking the queenside) or …f5 (central counter); White storms with g4 once the rook and knight are in place.

playableLines.title: The Ra3-g3 rook lift onto the closed center
annotations: …c4 — Black clamps the queenside, but closing that wing only frees White to throw everything at the king.
axb5 — White cracks open the a-file before launching the rook-swing.
…axb5 — Black recaptures; the a-file is open, but White's rook is already heading the other way.
Nd4 — the knight leaps to d4, clamping c6 and clearing f3 for the Ra3-g3 swing at the king.
learnCues: Nd4 — clear the path to g3

title: Zaitsev: Tension into Technique
overview: Karpov's lifelong weapon. Black commits the bishop to b7 and the rook to e8, holding the centre at maximum tension — and here the bishop stays on b3, because the ...Bb7 setup never goes for the Noah's Ark. White plays the quiet a3 and waits; whichever way the tension breaks, the resulting structure favours White's technique.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Clamp the centre and define the structure for the technical phase.
Restrain and then pressure the queenside before trading down.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: Black's ...Re8 backs the centre; White's a-file play targets the queenside in the ending.
Black's regroup to f8 reinforces the king; White keeps the bishop pair as the long-term trump.

strategicThemes: Hold the central tension; the side that resolves it on better terms owns the ending.
Here the bishop stays on b3 — the ...Bb7 setup never threatens Noah's Ark, so no retreat is needed.
White's bishop pair and central space are the technical trumps when the position simplifies.
endgameTransitions: Once the tension breaks, an ending with the bishop pair and more space tends to favour White.
Precise move-order is everything — a single tempo decides whether the simplification helps or hurts.

annotations: The Zaitsev — Black commits the bishop to b7 and the rook to e8, holding the centre at maximum tension. Note the bishop stays on b3: the ...Bb7 plan never targets it, so there's no Noah's Ark to dodge here.
a3 — quiet prophylaxis, taking the b4-square from Black's pieces before the centre resolves.

The tension will break with d5 or ...exd4. Either way the position simplifies toward an ending where White's central space and the bishop pair are the lasting edge. Zaitsev is razor theory that, played accurately, drifts into White's favour in the endgame.
playableLines.title: Maximum Tension, then the Better Structure

title: Scandinavian: Patient Gubinsky Solidity
overview: The …Qd8 Gubinsky-Melts: the queen home and the position impregnable. Black has the light bishop active on the b1-h7 diagonal and a solid, French-like structure with no target. The plan is patience — complete development, keep the bishop strong, and exploit White's g4-style loosening of his own king over the long term.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The Caro-like wall gives Black a structure with no weaknesses, the foundation of the …Qd8 Gubinsky-Melts.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: Black swaps the bishop for the knight to reach a low-risk, weakness-free position.
After White’s g4, the queen exploits the holes and offers a trade.

No weaknesses to attack
Target White's loosened kingside
endgameTransitions: The sound structure favours Black if White over-extends

…Qd5! Black centralizes the queen, offering a trade and exploiting the holes g4 created. This is the Gubinsky-Melts blueprint: trade pieces, build the c6-e6 wall, and let White's over-extension become the target. Carlsen outplayed Caruana from exactly this footing.

title: Scandinavian: The Icelandic Initiative
overview: The Icelandic Gambit throws a pawn at the centre for a roaring lead in development. Black's pieces flood out — …Nc6, …Bc5 raking f2, …Qd7 and …O-O-O connecting the rooks on the half-open files, then …Bg4 to pin the f3-knight. The initiative, not the pawn count, is Black's currency.

Long castling onto the open files
Pin and pressure the f3-knight
endgameTransitions: If the initiative fades the missing pawn tells, so Black must keep attacking

title: Scandinavian Main: …O-O-O and the …f5 Break
overview: In the …Qc7 main line Black has already solved the problem bishop with …Bf5-g6. Now the king goes long, and once White swaps off the g6-bishop the half-open h-file becomes Black's. Then …f5 strikes in the centre, opening the position for the well-placed pieces. Active development is the through-line of the whole Scandinavian.

The half-open h-file after the g6-trade
Open the centre with …f5
endgameTransitions: The sound structure holds an easy balance if the attack stalls

title: Modern Scandinavian: Active Knights vs the Doubled Pawns
overview: Where the opening leaves off — Black has traded the fianchetto bishop to plant two centralized knights and saddle White with doubled c-pawns (c3 and c5). The knights on d5 and c6 hit White’s queen and screen the board; the plan is to undermine c5 with …b6, fix c3, and let dynamic piece play press the weak pawns. Compensation is activity, not material.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The engine-backed continuation — Nxc3 is the strong move in this position, carrying out the plan above.

strategicThemes: Black’s centralized knights on d5 and c6 are the compensation — active, hitting the white queen and dominating the centre.
White’s doubled c-pawns (c3 and c5) are the targets: …b6 undermines c5, …axb6 fixes c3 as a permanent weakness.
Black plays for dynamics, not the structure — open lines for the pieces and trade into a position where the weak c3-pawn tells.

title: Portuguese Scandinavian: Active Queen and the …e5 Break
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Portuguese gambit has simplified into a balanced middlegame. Black’s queen is active on f5, the structure is sound, and White’s f3 has loosened the light squares. The plan is straightforward: finish developing, pin the c3-knight, and break in the centre with …e5 (or …c5), pressing the squares White weakened.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The engine-backed continuation — Qc5+ is the strong move in this position, carrying out the plan above.

strategicThemes: Black’s queen is active on f5 and the structure is sound — the position is equal, and Black completes development with tempo.
White’s f3 has weakened the light squares (e3, g3); Black’s pieces and the …e5/…c5 breaks press that soft complex.
A central majority and the active queen give Black comfortable, slightly easier play in a symmetrical-material middlegame.

playableLines.title: Pin, then break with …e5

…Qc6 — the queen regroups to c6, still gnawing at c4 and the airy squares near the white king.

title: Scandinavian …Qa5: the Opposite-Castling Race
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the …Qa5 mainline with kings castled on opposite wings. It is a race: White attacks Black’s kingside, Black storms the white king on b1. Black already has the queen on a5 and the bishop on b4 aimed at c3 — the knight shielding the king. The plan is …b5-b4, ripping open the b- and c-files. Speed beats material.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The engine-backed break — b5 is the principled continuation here, gaining ground in the structure the plan describes.

strategicThemes: Opposite-side castling means a race — Black attacks the white king on b1 while White goes for Black’s kingside; whoever arrives first wins.
Black storms with …b5-b4 to pry open the b- and c-files; the queen on a5 and bishop on b4 are already trained on c3.
The …Bxc3 break removes the knight shielding the white king — the standard Scandinavian attacking motif.

…exf5 — Black recaptures, opening the e-file at White's centre while the b-pawn keeps rolling.

title: Scandinavian: The Flexible …Qd6 Setup
overview: The Tiviakov …Qd6 with …a6 prophylaxis and …Bg4 pin. The queen sits flexible and untouchable on d6; Black develops harmoniously, pins the f3-knight, and castles long onto the d-file. The plan is patient and sound — pressure the centre, complete development, and break with …e5 when ready.

Pin and pressure
Sound development
endgameTransitions: The weakness-free structure holds comfortably

title: Schliemann: Develop with the Initiative
overview: The Schliemann's compensation for its loosened structure is pure activity: the open f-file, a lead in development, and the bishop pair. In the sharp main line Black regains the sacrificed material and, even when White grabs a pawn on the rim, gets a thoroughly active position. The plan is to develop fast with tempo, target any offside white piece, and use the open f-file against the white king.

title: Four Knights: Press the Hanging d5-Pawn
overview: The Scotch Four Knights middlegame: a near-symmetrical structure where White leans on Black's split queenside pawns and the d5-point with Bg5 and a knight rerouted via e2 to g3 toward f5. Quiet, classical, structure-driven chess.

title: Scotch Gambit: the f5/e5 Pawn Storm
overview: Where the opening leaves off — a Scotch Gambit structure where White owns a broad e4/f4 pawn centre and a development lead. The plan is direct: roll the centre with f5 and e5, prying open lines at the black king, while the Bb5 pins the c6-knight. Space and initiative, pressed toward an attack.

overview: The Classical Scotch middlegame: White trades the centralised knight and the dark-squared bishops to saddle Black with doubled c-pawns, then claims kingside space with f4 and pins the c6-knight with Bb5. A clean, Capablanca-style plan — convert the healthier structure.

overview: White keeps the e5-pawn — the cramping wedge that defines the Mieses — clamps with c4 to grab queenside space and kick the d5-knight, props it with b3, and expands with f4. Black blockades on d5 and hits back with …d6, but White's space gives a durable, comfortable pull.

White just develops — O-O, Rb1 — and the lead in development plus the exposed king are a lasting plus.

title: Semi-Slav Botvinnik: Extra Pawns and the Rolling c-Pawns
overview: Where the opening leaves off — deep in the razor-sharp Botvinnik Semi-Slav, where Black has grabbed material (the d4-pawn) and holds the c4-pawn, banking on the bishops and the connected queenside pawns. The plan is concrete: consolidate the king, keep the extra material, and roll the c-pawns. White has activity and the open lines; precision decides everything.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The c-pawns connect and roll — …c5 backs up the passed c4-pawn, building a queenside steamroller that is Black’s long-term winning chance.

The g7- and b7-bishops rake the long diagonals; White’s compensation is activity and the open files for the pawns.

title: Alapin …d5 — blockade the IQP, outlast the activity
overview: The …d5 antidote has done its structural work: White carries the isolated d4-pawn, and everything he owns points at our king to justify it. Honesty first — the engine leans White by two-thirds here, the IQP's activity at its peak. The classical defusal is the plan: rook to d8 against the pawn, knight to the d5 blockade, and when the e3-bishop offers itself, trade and re-lean with …Bf6. Every trade ages the isolani; our job is reaching the ending where it answers for itself.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The knight sits where the isolani wants to advance; everything else follows from that.
The rook loads against d4 before the blockade lands — order matters.
After the trade on e3, the bishop re-aims at the pawn the blockade fixed.

strategicThemes: IQP defence is a schedule: siege first, blockade second, trades third.
Trade the pieces that attack; keep the pieces that besiege.

endgameTransitions: The isolated d4-pawn answers for itself in every ending — simplification IS the plan.

title: Alapin Main: Blockade the Isolated d4-Pawn
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Alapin IQP, where White’s isolated d4-pawn gives space and piece activity in return for a long-term weakness. Black’s plan is the textbook IQP fight: blockade the pawn with a knight on d5, trade off White’s attacking pieces, and grind toward an endgame where the isolani falls. Watch White’s Qg4 for kingside tricks.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The knight reroutes to d5, the perfect blockading square in front of the isolated pawn — it can never be driven off by a pawn, and from there it dominates.

The blockading square is d5: a knight there can never be chased by a pawn and smothers White’s dynamism.

title: Chinese Dragon: the …Rb8/…b5-b4 Storm
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Chinese Dragon, where Black puts the rook on b8 behind the b-pawn and storms. With kings on opposite wings it is a race: White attacks the kingside, Black tears open the queenside. …b5-b4 hits the c3-knight that shields the white king, the g7-bishop rakes the long diagonal, and the open files do the rest.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The engine-backed continuation — Rb7 is the strong move in this position, carrying out the plan above.

strategicThemes: Opposite-side castling makes it a race — Black storms the white king on c1 while White attacks the kingside; speed is everything.
The …Rb8/…b5-b4 storm hits the c3-knight shielding the king; …a5-a4 reinforces it.
The g7-bishop rakes the long diagonal at c3 and b2 — when the pawns crash through, it is already aimed at the king.

playableLines.title: …b5-b4 against the c1-king
annotations: Ndxb5 — White snatches the b5-pawn, but cracking open the b-file is playing with fire against the Dragon.
…Rb7 — the signature Chinese-Dragon lift: the rook loads the half-open b-file, ready to double behind the queen.
Nd4 — White scurries the knight back to d4, but the b-file is already a battering ram.
…Qb8 — the queen swings in behind the rook; the whole battery bears down the b-file at the white king.

title: Classical Dragon: The …d5 Central Break
overview: In the quiet Classical (Be2) Dragon there is no Yugoslav-Attack storm to fear, so Black plays for the centre. The plan is patient: mass …Be6, …Qc8, …Rd8 behind the d-file, then strike with the freeing …d5 break that liberates the whole position. Reaching …d5 is the Classical Dragon's whole point.

pawnBreaks.explanation: After …Be6/…Qc8/…Rd8 mass behind it, …d5 strikes the centre and frees Black’s game; even e5 in reply meets …Ne4 with active play.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The queen steps off the d-file so the rook can back the coming …d5.

pieceManeuvers.route: …Rf8-d8 — load the d-file behind the break
pieceManeuvers.explanation: The rook swings to d8, lining up directly behind the …d5 break.

strategicThemes: No kingside storm to fear in the quiet Classical
Mass …Be6/…Qc8/…Rd8 behind the centre
Free the game with the …d5 break
endgameTransitions: With the centre freed, Black’s active pieces hold the balance into the endgame

title: Classical Dragon: Queenside Expansion and Pressure on e4
overview: Where the opening leaves off — a Classical Dragon where both sides castled kingside, so it is a positional fight rather than a race. Black expands on the queenside with …b5-a5-b4 and trains his pieces on e4: the c5-knight and the g7-bishop both press it, and trading off White’s light-squared bishop softens the light squares.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The queenside expansion — …b5-b4 gains space and drives the c3-knight, loosening White’s grip on the centre and the e4-pawn.
The freeing central break — once Black’s pieces press e4, …d5 strikes the centre and opens the position for the g7-bishop.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The knight on c5 pressures e4 and eyes the b3/d3 outposts; trading off White’s d3-bishop weakens his light squares.

strategicThemes: Both kings are on the kingside — this is a positional Dragon, not a race; Black plays on the queenside and against e4.
Black expands with …b5-a5-b4, gaining space and driving the c3-knight that guards the centre.
The c5-knight and g7-bishop both press e4; trading White’s d3-bishop softens the light squares for the …d5 break.

title: Yugoslav Dragon: the …Rxc3 Exchange Sacrifice
overview: Where the opening leaves off — deep in the Yugoslav Attack, the sharpest race in chess. Black’s whole plan is the …Rxc3 exchange sacrifice: give up the rook for the knight that shields White’s king, shatter the b- and c-pawns, and pour the queen and the g7-bishop down the long diagonal and the open c-file. It is a pure race; the side that breaks through first wins.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The engine-backed continuation — Bxg4 is the strong move in this position, carrying out the plan above.

strategicThemes: The Yugoslav Attack is a pure opposite-wing race — Black must crash through on the queenside before White’s h-file attack lands.
The …Rxc3 exchange sacrifice is the engine of Black’s attack: it removes the knight shielding the king and shatters the pawn cover.
The g7-bishop rakes the long diagonal at c3 and b2; once the pawns fall it bears straight down on the white king.

…e5 — the spear thrust: …e5 kicks the d4-knight and unleashes the g7-bishop down the long diagonal at the king.

title: Soltis: Freeze the Storm, then Strike
overview: The Soltis plan: meet White's h4 with h5, nailing the kingside shut, then turn the full force of the c-file and the c4-knight against White's king with no counterplay coming the other way.

pawnBreaks.explanation: h5 freezes White's h-pawn and kills the entire kingside storm before it begins.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: Once the kingside is locked, the knight jumps to c4 to spearhead the attack.

strategicThemes: h5 neutralises White's whole reason for castling long.
With the storm frozen, Black attacks for free.
The c-file and the c4-knight do the work.
endgameTransitions: A frozen kingside leaves Black pressing risk-free on the queenside.

title: Najdorf 6.a4: Central Play and the c5-Outpost
overview: White’s 6.a4 clamps the queenside and rules out …b5, so Black turns to the centre and pieces. The d7-knight reroutes to the c5-outpost — immune to a pawn and hitting e4 — while the rooks swing to c8 and e8 to press White’s centre. Roughly level with comfortable, natural counterplay for Black.

endgameTransitions: The outpost knight and central control hold the balance

title: Najdorf 6.g3: …Nc5, …b5 and the d5 Break
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the fianchetto Najdorf with Black’s e5/d6 Boleslavsky centre. The fight is over d5: White wants a knight there, Black wants the …d5 break. Meanwhile Black expands on the queenside — …Nc5 hits e4, …b5 strikes the a4-pawn and opens lines for the b8-rook. Patient Najdorf two-front play.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The engine-backed break — b6 is the principled continuation here, gaining ground in the structure the plan describes.

strategicThemes: Black’s e5/d6 Boleslavsky centre fixes the struggle on d5 — White angles a knight onto it, Black works toward the …d5 break.
On the queenside Black expands with …Nc5 (hitting e4) and …b5 (hitting a4), opening files for the b8-rook.
…d5 is the freeing central break; until it lands, Black plays on the wing and presses e4.

title: Najdorf Classical: Trade the d5-Knight, Press the Queenside
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the Classical Najdorf with White’s knight planted on d5. Black’s first job is to challenge that outpost (…Bxd5) and then turn to the queenside: …a5-a4 harasses the b3-knight, …b5 opens lines, and a knight reroutes to c4. Trade the strong d5-knight, then play against White’s loosening queenside.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Gains queenside space and drives at the b3-knight — …a5-a4 forces it to a passive square and clamps White’s queenside.
The thematic Najdorf expansion — …b5 opens the b-file and gains space for the queenside minority once the d5-knight has been traded.

overview: The English Attack race: White storms with g4-g5, Black answers with b5 and b4, prising open the b-file at the long-castled king. Black's attack is famously fast. (The 6.f3 move order transposes into this same English Attack race.)

title: Sveshnikov 9.Bxf6: Bishop Pair and the …f5-f4 Roll
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the sharp Sveshnikov where White took on f6 to plant a knight on d5, leaving Black with doubled f-pawns but the bishop pair and the …f5 thrust already on the board. Black’s trumps are the two bishops and kingside space: …f5-f4 rolls forward, …b4 expands the queenside, and …Ne7 challenges the d5-knight.

title: Sveshnikov Chelyabinsk: Dark Bishop, …Bg5 and the …f5 Break

title: Slav: The …e5 Central Break
overview: Black brings the light-squared bishop out to f5, lets White post the knight on e5 and win the c4-pawn back, then frees the whole position with the …e5 central break — the mainstream way the Slav equalizes. The point isn't a one-move trick; it's that …e5 liberates every black piece at once.

title: Classical Vienna: the f5 Outpost Attack
overview: Where the opening leaves off — the knight planted on f5, the bishop reloaded on c2. White’s middlegame is a kingside attack organised around the f5 outpost: the queen lifts to d3 to double with the bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal, the e5 break opens lines toward the black king, and if Black challenges the knight with …g6 the h-pawn joins the storm. Black’s one freeing counter is …d5. The chances are balanced, but White’s attack is the easier side to play.

pawnBreaks.explanation: White’s central break. The pawn strikes d6 and clears e4 off the b1-h7 diagonal, so the f5-knight and the Bc2–Qd3 battery both fire toward the black king.

Black’s freeing counter-break, hitting e4 and the f5-knight’s support. White meets it with exd5 (or pre-empts with e5) so Black never frees the position for free — this is the break White must always be ready for.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The queen lifts to d3, doubling with the c2-bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal. Behind the f5-knight, the battery points straight at h7 — the engine of the kingside attack.
The knight sits on f5 permanently — no Black pawn can chase it (Lasker’s rule). From f5 it presses d6 and h6 and screens the attack; if …g6 ever hits it, h4-h5 pries the kingside open.

strategicThemes: The knight on f5 is a permanent outpost (Lasker) — it presses d6 and h6 and anchors the entire kingside attack.
Queen d3 plus bishop c2 form a battery on the b1-h7 diagonal; the e5 break removes White’s own e4-pawn from that diagonal and trains it on h7.
If Black plays …g6 to challenge the f5-knight, White answers with h4-h5, using the pawn to pry open the h-file rather than retreating the knight for free.
Black’s only equaliser is …d5 — White times e5, or answers …d5 with exd5, so Black never frees the centre without a concession.

overview: The symmetric mirror: both sides fianchetto, castle short, and stake the c- and e-pawns. The d6-bishop is Black's good piece; trading it is the point of the whole maneuver.
Small, stable edges: bishop pair plus a hole beats a flashy attack here.
endgameTransitions: The bishop-pair edge grows as pieces come off — steer for the two-bishop ending.

annotations: …e5 — Black plants a pawn on e5. A proud centre — but d5 is soft behind it, and no black pawn can ever guard that square again.

playableLines.title: The c4 Question
playableLines.intro: The knight lands on c4 and the d6-bishop has no good answer — the trade leaves White the bishop pair and the d5 hole.

title: KIA into KID — the space clamp
overview: When the move order becomes a genuine King's Indian, he takes the White side of the space clamp — twenty-nine of his games run through this junction, twenty wins against eight. The d5-e4 pawn duo cramps Black; the plan is patience: back the e4-pawn, lay the b3-a3 base, and only then hit the c5-knight with b4. The engine calls it level — but the space means White chooses where the game happens.

pawnBreaks.move: b3, a3, then b4 — the queenside base
pawnBreaks.explanation: Two quiet pawn moves prepare the one that matters: b4 kicks the c5-knight and rolls the queenside.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The rook backs e4 so the c5-knight's pressure comes to nothing.

strategicThemes: The d5-e4 duo is the whole position — defend it, then expand.
Answer wing probes with one pawn move, never a concession.
Time matters: Black's knight detour to h6 is exactly the tempo b4 needs.
endgameTransitions: If the queenside opens on White's terms, the space edge becomes a passed-pawn race White starts first.

annotations: …Nc5 — the d7-knight jumps to c5, hitting the e4-pawn head-on.
Re1 — the rook steps behind the e-pawn. The pressure on e4 is answered before it becomes real.
…b6 — Black shores up the c5 square before b4 can kick the knight.

…Ng4 — the f6-knight probes g4, sniffing at the dark squares around White's king.

…Nh6 — back it goes, to the rim. The detour costs Black exactly the time White wanted.

playableLines.title: The Space Clamp
playableLines.intro: A real King's Indian with him on the space side — defend e4, build b3-a3, then b4 hits the knight.

title: Rossolimo proper — open the centre, then clamp with c4
overview: Black solved the Rossolimo with ...d5, and the corpus answer is to let the trade happen and take the centre back with d4. From this position the engine confirms what the structure suggests: develop with Be3, recapture on d4, and then the real point — c4, fixing Black's queenside majority in place before it ever moves. The bind arrives one move at a time, and every move is a developing move.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The clamp: c4 freezes the c5-square complex and turns Black's extra queenside pawn into a bystander.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: Be3 hits c5 immediately — the bishop develops by asking Black's most advanced pawn a question.
The knights take the central squares the pawn trade vacated — d4 first, then c3 backing the clamp.

strategicThemes: Trade the d-pawns, keep the initiative: White's pieces arrive first to the open board.
The c4 clamp against the a6/b7 majority — space now, endgame pressure later.
endgameTransitions: The better structure tells into the endgame.

annotations: The bishop develops with a threat — c5 is attacked, and Black's choice is trade or defend, both of which speed White's plan.
Black trades rather than defend a pawn that was always going to be a target.
The knight recaptures into the centre. Count the activity: knight on d4, bishop on e3, rook already on e1 — against three developed Black pieces and a queenside asleep.

title: Taimanov transposition — Nb3 and the dark-square trade
overview: When Black ducks the Rossolimo with ...e6, the game opens like a Kan — and the corpus answer is direct: meet the bishop's arrival on c5 with Nb3, then trade it off on a7 and keep the better structure. Five games, five wins in his corpus from this hit. Without the dark-squared bishop, Black's whole ...a6/...e6 setup loses its teeth: the d6-square softens and White develops with the initiative.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: Be3 offers the trade the position wants: after Bxa7 Rxa7, Black's rook stands offside and the dark squares belong to White.

strategicThemes: Trade the dark-squared bishops and Black's Kan setup loses its best piece.
The a7-rook: winning the trade ON a7 drags the rook to a square it never wanted.
endgameTransitions: The small edge holds into the endgame.

annotations: The bishop ducks to a7 to keep its diagonal — but watch what that costs the rook behind it.
The queen steps to e2, connecting the pieces and keeping d1 free for a rook.
The knight develops inside the shell — Black's setup is solid but slow.
Be3 offers the trade. Black cannot decline forever: the bishops stare at each other down the same diagonal.
Black castles first, hoping the question goes away.
It does not: the trade lands on a7, and the recapture is the point of the whole line —
— the rook is dragged to a7, one square off the board's edge, needing two moves to matter again.

playableLines.title: The dark-square trade
playableLines.intro: His five-for-five treatment of the ...e6 duck: hit the bishop, trade it on a7, keep the squares.

title: Bxd7+ Trade — the e5 wedge and the Rc1–c3 lift
overview: Trade the bishops early and the position tells you the rest: his games walk this exact French-style structure — e5 wedge, open c-file — over twenty times, scoring nearly three to one. The plan is the rook lift you would never find by accident: Rc1, then Rc3, where the rook watches the c-file and stands one slide from the kingside. Space plus the more flexible rook is the whole story.

pawnBreaks.explanation: A quiet clamp — a3 takes b4 from Black's knight and rook before the queenside opens.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The corpus lift: the rook takes the open file, then the third rank — pressing c6 today, ready to swing kingside tomorrow.

strategicThemes: The e5 wedge cramps the kingside knight-less French structure — Black's pieces queue behind three pawns.
Play on both sides: the c-file rook converts to a kingside attacker in one move.
endgameTransitions: The pull persists into the endgame.

annotations: Black develops and prepares to castle — the structure is a French without light-squared bishops, which suits White's space.
The rook claims the only open file before Black's rooks are ready to argue about it.
Black tucks the king away. Nothing is loose yet — but nothing is active either.
The lift: Rc3. On the third rank the rook does two jobs — it leans on the file, and it stands one move from g3 or h3 if the king ever invites it.
Black contests the file, exactly as the position demands.

And a3 — the little clamp his games play here. The b4-square is gone, the queenside is sealed, and White keeps both plans alive while Black has only the wait. Fourteen wins to five in his corpus from this structure.
learnCues: a3 — seal it, keep both plans.
playableLines.title: The rook-lift conversion
playableLines.intro: His twenty-two-game continuation from the Bxd7+ terminus: wedge, file, lift, clamp.

title: Adams Attack — consolidate, then trade the intruder
overview: The h3 Adams Attack aims for g4 and a slow squeeze; the answer is consolidation with teeth. From the …h5 tabiya — the move that fights for g4 before White gets it — the plan runs: meet Be3 with …Be6, and when the knight lands on d5, trade it off immediately and collect the check on a5. The engine reads under a fifth of a pawn for White — the Adams defused, and Black's game plays itself from there.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The bishop develops onto the knight's landing square and removes the octopus the moment it arrives.

pieceManeuvers.route: d8 → a5, with check — the free move
pieceManeuvers.explanation: The recapture structure hands Black a check — a whole tempo the defence banks.

strategicThemes: …h5 fights for g4 before White's whole setup gets its point.
Trade the d5 intruder the move it lands — hesitation is what the Adams feeds on.
Checks are tempi: …Qa5+ turns defence into free development.
endgameTransitions: The d5-pawn wedge left after the trade is a target in every ending — blockade, then besiege.

…Be6 — and we develop onto d5, the square White's whole plan runs through.
Nd5 — the knight lands anyway —
…Bxd5 — and leaves immediately. The intruder is traded the move it arrives; that timing is the entire defence.
exd5 — White recaptures and the structure fixes.
…Qa5+ — the free move: check, and the queen arrives on its best Najdorf square with tempo.
Nc3 — White must block.
…Nbd7 — development completes at leisure. Under a fifth of a pawn on the engine — the Adams Attack defused into a position where Black's moves play themselves.
playableLines.title: Trade the Intruder
playableLines.intro: …h5 first, then the drill: bishop to e6, take the knight the moment it lands, collect the check.

title: Two Knights — the Rubinstein …Nd4
overview: When White declines the Alekhine with Nc3 and reaches for the Spanish pin, his corpus answer is emphatic: at the Bb5 position he plays the Rubinstein …Nd4 in 103 of 132 games. The plan from the tabiya is a chain of clean trades — knights on d4, bishops on e6 — and the punchline recapture …fxe6, opening the f-file for the castled rook. The engine puts Black a fifth of a pawn AHEAD at the end of the line.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Recapturing toward the centre opens the f-file for the rook that castled onto it, and the e6-d6 pawns rule the central light squares.

pieceManeuvers.route: c5 × d4 → b6 — never off the diagonal
pieceManeuvers.explanation: The bishop recaptures in the centre and, when challenged, slides to b6 still staring at f2.

strategicThemes: The Rubinstein …Nd4 turns White's Spanish pin into a target.
Trade into the structure you want: the …fxe6 recapture is a gain, not a concession.
A bishop that never leaves its diagonal loses nothing by stepping back.
endgameTransitions: The half-open f-file and the f2 target carry straight into any ending — rook activity decides these.

annotations: Nxd4 — White finally removes the centralized knight.
…Bxd4 — recapture with the bishop, which now sits beautifully in the centre of the board.
O-O — White tucks the king away.
…Be6 — develop and offer the c4-bishop a trade on our terms.
Bxe6 — White takes —
…fxe6 — and THIS recapture is the point: the f-file opens in front of our castled rook, and the e6-d6 pawn pair rules the central light squares.
Ne2 — the knight challenges our proud d4-bishop.
…Bb6 — keep it. The bishop steps back but never leaves the a7-g1 diagonal — still staring at f2. A fifth of a pawn better for BLACK out of the opening: the Rubinstein, delivered.

title: c4 Modern — the solid wall vs the space
overview: The corpus route through the c4 Modern castles early and regroups the queenside knight via a6 to c7 — five games reached this exact tabiya, five wins for Black. White's extra space is real: the engine leans just over half a pawn his way. The plan is what makes the line playable anyway — the b6-knight re-routes through d7 to f6, the rook takes the open e-file, and the position offers White nothing to bite on. Space against solidity; his score says solidity.

pieceManeuvers.route: b6 → d7 → f6 — the kingside re-route
pieceManeuvers.explanation: The queenside knight walks across to f6, covering the king and watching the e4-square White's pawns left behind.
Both e-pawns are gone; the rook takes the fully open file before White's do.

strategicThemes: Space is only an advantage if there is something to attack — give White nothing.
The e-file is fully open; claiming it first is worth more than a pawn-storm gesture.
Trust the record: engine says White leans, his five-for-five score says the setup holds.
endgameTransitions: In the ending White's extra space becomes extra squares to defend — the d4-c4 pawns want constant babysitting.

…h6 — a useful hedge: g5 is denied to the c1-bishop before it ever asks.
Bf4 — the bishop takes the h2-b8 diagonal, leaning on our d6-pawn.
…Re8 — the rook claims the fully open e-file. Both e-pawns left the board long ago; the file belongs to whoever moves first, and that is us.

title: Nf3 Quiet — the c-pawn recapture and the long hold
overview: Honesty first: in the Quiet line the engine leans White by most of a pawn after best play — that is this sideline's toll, and the narration won't pretend otherwise. What the number doesn't show is why he plays it anyway: seventeen wins to eight in the corpus. The …cxd6 recapture keeps the structure compact, everything castles, and …a5-a4 generates real queenside counterplay against the b3-queen. A defensible fighting line you must know — not a free lunch.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The pawn march harasses the b3-queen and fixes White's queenside before it expands.

strategicThemes: Recapture toward the centre: …cxd6 keeps the pawn wall compact and the c-file half-open.
When the engine leans against you, play the structures your results support.
Counterplay is a duty, not a luxury — …a5 starts it before White consolidates.
endgameTransitions: The compact d6-e6 structure survives simplification well — trades relieve the space toll.

…a5 — and Black's counterplay starts on schedule: a4 comes next, harassing that queen. The engine leans White by most of a pawn here — the Quiet line's honest toll — but the structure holds together, the counterplay is real, and his corpus in this variation reads seventeen wins to eight.

title: Steinitz — centre held, develop and press
overview: Against the old …d6 Steinitz the d4 break has already landed, and the plan is a model of classical patience: castle, put the rook behind the e-pawn, tuck the Spanish bishop to c2 where it keeps its diagonal, and develop the last bishop with an eye on d8. The engine gives half a pawn — the Steinitz's permanent tax for solidity — and every White move in the line is one you would find on principle alone.

The Spanish bishop's retreat to c2 is a promise, not a concession — the diagonal reopens when the centre clarifies.
Half a pawn of space, permanently: the Steinitz gives it and cannot take it back.

title: e6 French Setup — the Bxd6 trade and the level fight
overview: Against the solid ...e6 setup the corpus is honest: trade on d6 the moment the bishop appears, accept the symmetric structure, and outplay from equal. His forty-plus games with Bd3 here show the shape — the c-file half-open for Black, the e5-square soft for White — and the engine calls it dead level. The plan is the knight reroute: Nd2 to b3, clamping c5 and a5, castling behind it, and meeting Black's ...e5 space with the e4 stop. No advantage to protect — just better middlegame moves.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The reroute: from b3 the knight owns c5 and a5, and the f-file stays clear for the rook after f3 or f4 later.

strategicThemes: An honestly level structure: play it for the middlegame, not the eval bar.
Clamp the dark squares (b3-knight, c5) while Black's counterplay needs ...e5 — then fix it with e4.
endgameTransitions: A pawn up, trades favour White.

Castle. With the clamp in place there is no rush; the game is long.
When the pawn comes to e4 the position fixes: Black has space, White has the c5 square and the sounder pawns. His games grind exactly this — the player with the plan wins the level position.

title: Slav Style — the bishop question and the b4 gain

Castle, put the rook behind the e-pawn, and when the bishop check comes, walk it backward with a3 and b4: every step of the chase gains queenside space Black never recovers. His ten corpus games ride this quiet edge; the engine calls it a clean, riskless plus for White.

title: a6 with ...c5 — the e4 break
overview: The ...a6/...c5 system trades on d4 and develops smoothly — and the corpus answer arrives on one move: e4, the central break his games play from exactly this position at seven wins to two. The break trades a pair of knights and the d5-pawn's pride, and what remains is the position White wanted all along: the raking d3-bishop, the freer game, and a target on e6 that never heals.

title: KIA vs Modern — a4 stop and the c4 probe
overview: The Modern move order lands in the same symmetric fight — twenty-five of his games run through this tabiya, fifteen wins against six. Two habits do the work: a4 the moment Black grabs wing space, freezing the a5-pawn where it stands, and then the queen's knight to c4, where it leans on e5 and d6. The engine calls it near-level; the maneuvering game is his home turf.

Mirror structures reward the player with the clearer plan — that's the point of learning this one.

title: Steinitz — the d5 clamp

title: Bc4 vs ...d6 — the Italian slow build

title: vs ...g6 — the Na3–b5 tour and the wrecked queenside

title: Caro Exchange — the …Bg4 antidote holds
overview: The Exchange Variation's classic antidote, fully deployed: bishop out to g4 before …e6, queen on d6, everything castled. White's Qb3 prod is met by the rook simply guarding b7, and when the knight leaps to e5 the bishop sidesteps to h5 rather than concede. The engine reads a fifth of a pawn for White — the Exchange Caro's whole story: White gets the first pull, and Black's setup absorbs it move after move.

strategicThemes: The half-open c-file belongs to Black in every Exchange Caro — claim it early.
Answer prods with the quietest sufficient move; …Rab8 defuses Qb3 completely.
Absorb, don't chase: White's initiative spends itself against a wall with no cracks.
endgameTransitions: The symmetrical d-pawn structure makes every ending holdable; the c-file rook usually ends up the better one.

…Qc7 — the queen slides behind the c-file rook, leaning on the e5-knight through d6. A fifth of a pawn for White says the engine — and not one crack in the wall for it to work on.

title: Caro Classical — castle into the h5 squeeze, and hold
overview: The Classical main line at full depth: White has the h5 space squeeze and the long castle; Black has the structure with no holes. The plan takes nerve, which is why it must be KNOWN rather than found: castle short directly into the squeeze, recapture on f6 with the knight, and fire the …c5 break the moment White's king commits. When the g4 lunge comes — and it comes — take it. The engine holds the balance at a shade for White; panic is the only way to lose the Classical.

pawnBreaks.explanation: The counter in the centre answers White's wing ambitions — standard doctrine, precise timing.

strategicThemes: The h5 squeeze looks scarier than it is — the g6 square is covered and the files stay shut.
Opposite-side kings: White's g4 lunge is an invitation; taking it is the engine's move.

endgameTransitions: If queens trade on the d-file the h5-pawn turns from a squeeze into a weakness — remember which side of that trade you are.

…c5 — so the break fires on schedule: the centre answers the wing, as it always must.
g4 — the lunge. White offers a real pawn to rip open the g-file.

…Nxg4 — take it. The engine holds the line at a shade for White — the Classical Caro's standing bargain: they get the look of an attack, we get the pawn and the structure. Panic is the only losing move.

overview: The line every Trompowsky player prays for: Black grabbed b2, chased material through the complications, and the corpus line arrives here with the engine reading plus five and a half. This plan is memorized, not discovered: know the sequence and the …Qxb2 grab becomes a scoresheet you have already read.

title: English vs …e5 — the bishop pair holds
overview: The reversed-Sicilian line ends with the tension resolved and the truth on the table: Black gave up the dark-squared bishop back on move five, and everything White does from here is built on owning the pair. The engine calls the finish dead level — but level with two bishops against bishop and knight is the kind of level this repertoire is happy to grind.

title: English Symmetric — Rb1 and the half-open b-file
overview: Pure symmetry — both sides fianchetto, both castle, the pawns mirror. The way to play these is to bank tiny asymmetries before the position resolves: the rook steps to b1 off the g7-bishop's diagonal, b3 props c4, and when Black releases the tension with ...dxc4 the b-file opens with White's rook already standing on it. The engine says equal; the file says whose equal.

pawnBreaks.explanation: c4 is the one pawn under pressure; b3 holds it and readies the file-opening recapture.

pieceManeuvers.route: a1 → b1 — off the diagonal, onto the file
pieceManeuvers.explanation: One move, two jobs: the rook leaves the g7-bishop's x-ray and pre-claims the b-file.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The f6-knight holds Black's d5-tension together; Bg5 makes holding it uncomfortable.

strategicThemes: In symmetric positions, bank the small asymmetries before the structure resolves.
Pre-place the rook on the file that will open — never chase the file after the capture.
Pressure the piece that carries the opponent's pawn tension.

title: English vs …c6 — the b3 wall meets …e4
overview: The Slav-style ...c6 is the second-most-common reply he faces — 145 games in the corpus, 80 wins against 53 — met with the b3/Bb2 wall and quiet development. The critical moment comes when Black stakes everything on the ...e5-e4 space push: the knight drops into d4, the wedge gets liquidated on d3, and White emerges a shade better with the queen actively placed. Calm system chess against an ambitious lunge.

pawnBreaks.explanation: When the e4-pawn plants itself, d3 challenges it at once — liquidate the space grab before it becomes a bind.

pieceManeuvers.route: f3 → d4 — into the hole the push made

strategicThemes: A pawn that advances stops guarding the squares behind it — ...e4 donates d4.
Liquidate a space wedge before it calcifies into a bind.
System openings win by keeping the position honest: develop, castle, punish the lunge.

overview: When Black takes the gambit pawn, his corpus verdict is brutal: seventeen games, sixteen wins. The Accepted fails not to a refutation but to arithmetic — e5 sent the knight all the way home to g8, and by this tabiya every developed piece on the board is White's. title: Evans Gambit — the d4-e4 initiative
overview: The Evans at full stretch: a pawn invested, the d4-e4 centre standing, and every White piece pointed forward. The corpus continuation shows the gambit's machinery — Bb5 pins, Nd5 leaps at the b6-bishop, and the trade on b6 wrecks Black's queenside pawns before the bishop returns to its c4 diagonal. title: Jobava-London — the a4-knight probes c5
overview: The Jobava hybrid's mature middlegame: bishops traded on d6, the knight already re-routed to a4 by the opening. The plan is the probe — Nc5 lands on the square the exchange prepared, and when Black challenges it, the knight has b3, where it keeps watching both a5 and c5. Add the a4 space-stopper and the half-open e-file, and White holds a small, clean pull with zero weaknesses. The engine: a fifth of a pawn, all structure.

Then the knight takes e5 and bites that bishop immediately. Level on the engine; the outpost and the bad bishop are the two talking points that matter.

The e5 outpost gains value with every exchange around it.
endgameTransitions: A knight-on-e5 versus bad-bishop ending is the dream conversion — keep that trade map in mind.

annotations: …g6 — Black blunts the d3-bishop's diagonal before it ever bites.
Bb5 — so the bishop finds new work, leaning on the c6-knight.
…h5 — an ambitious jab: the pawn grabs space and hints at h4 against our g3-pawn.
Bxc6 — take. The recapture is forced to be awkward —
…Bxc6 — and there it is: the b7-bishop lands on c6, hemmed in by its own d5-pawn on the long diagonal.
Ne5 — the knight takes the outpost with tempo, biting the c6-bishop the moment it arrives.
…Rc8 — the rook slides across to babysit the bishop.

b4 — the queenside clamp: space gained, the c5-pawn asked the question. Level on the engine — but the outpost is ours and the bad bishop is theirs, and those are the two facts this middlegame is about.
playableLines.title: Bxc6 and the e5 Outpost
playableLines.intro: Trade so Black keeps the bad bishop, then land the knight on e5 with tempo.

title: London vs …c6 — the bishop keeps its diagonal
overview: The Slav-solid …c6 — 39 corpus games via the direct 2.Bf4 order — answered with the c4 break and a clean recapture. What follows is the London's oldest running joke: Black spends move after move chasing the f4-bishop with …Nh5 and …f6, and the bishop dances e5, then g3 — where taking it would open our h-file. Two-thirds of a pawn better, says the engine, mostly made of Black's spent tempi.

pieceManeuvers.route: f4 → e5 → g3 — the survival dance
pieceManeuvers.explanation: Chased by knight and pawn, the bishop steps through the CENTRE and lands where trading it opens the h-file for our rook.
The rook backs the e-pawn's future advance — which would hit the f5-bishop on its own diagonal.
When …Nb6 asks, the bishop simply goes home, conceding nothing.

strategicThemes: The London bishop is worth two tempi of chasing — make the chase cost exactly that.
Retreats that keep the piece on its best diagonal are not concessions.
If they trade on g3, the h-file opens with our rook already breathing on it.
endgameTransitions: Black's …f6 leaves e6 permanently tender — a target square for knight endings.

annotations: …Be7 — Black gets ready to castle.
Re1 — the rook slips behind the e-pawn, backing its future advance — an advance that would hit the f5-bishop, by the way.
…Nb6 — the d7-knight asks our c4-bishop the question.
Bf1 — the calm answer: straight home, conceding nothing, still watching the same diagonal from the back.
…Nh5 — and here comes the classic London question: the knight wants the f4-bishop.
Be5 — the classic answer: through the CENTRE, not backwards.
…f6 — kicked again, and now e6 is tender behind that pawn forever.
Bg3 — the dance ends on g3, where taking the bishop opens our h-file. Two-thirds of a pawn better — Black spent three moves chasing a bishop that finished exactly where it wanted to be.
playableLines.title: The Bishop Keeps Its Diagonal
playableLines.intro: Black chases the London bishop for three moves; it dances e5-g3 and ends up better placed than it started.

title: London vs KID — weather the counter, keep the pawn
overview: The anti-KID weapon has done its work: dark-square bishops traded through h6, our queen parked on h6, kings castled on opposite wings. Now Black lashes out — …d5, …Nc6, …Qa5 — and the plan is cold-blooded: take the c5-pawn when it's offered, block the a5-queen's path with Bb5, and spend one quiet move on a3 so nothing on b4 ever works. The engine gives White half a pawn; weather the storm and it stays won.

pawnBreaks.explanation: Black's attack runs on time, not material — banking the pawn makes his clock run faster.
One quiet move removes every …b4 and …Qb4 idea from the attack.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The bishop blocks the queenside light squares and hits the c6-knight in the same move.

strategicThemes: Opposite-side castling: his attack is queenside, ours already landed on h6 — material is the tiebreak.
Defend with moves that carry threats; Bb5 defends by attacking.
One prophylactic pawn move (a3) can be worth more than a rook lift.
endgameTransitions: Survive the queenside gusts and the extra pawn decides any ending.
