playableLines.title: Weather the Counter
playableLines.intro: Bank the offered pawn, block with tempo, and spend one quiet move killing the whole counterattack.

title: Main — the Qb3 bind, honestly priced
overview: Honesty first: at this tabiya the engine leans BLACK by a third of a pawn — the Ponziani's known price, and no narration here will pretend otherwise. What the number misses is why the line stays in the repertoire: at his corpus junction it scores four wins in five games, because over the board Black must solve problems the engine solves in silence. The plan takes the bishop pair with Bxc6, re-routes the queen to c2, and plays the structure out with confidence.

pieceManeuvers.route: b5 × c6 — take the pair's price
pieceManeuvers.explanation: The trade doubles Black's c-pawns and simplifies White's task — practical chess over engine chess.

pieceManeuvers.route: b3 → c2 — off the tempo squares
pieceManeuvers.explanation: The queen did its early work; c2 is where it stops paying rent.

strategicThemes: Play lines whose problems are harder for humans than engines — and say so out loud.
Doubled c-pawns plus the e5 cramp are real assets even when the eval isn't.
Know the price of your pet line, and make the opponent pay theirs first.
endgameTransitions: The doubled c-pawns give White the better pure pawn endings — steer trades that way when the middlegame stalls.

annotations: Bxc6+ — take with check: the doubled c-pawns arrive before Black finishes developing.
…bxc6 — the recapture; Black's queenside structure carries the mark for the rest of the game.
Qc2 — the queen's early adventure ends on a sensible square, off every tempo-gaining path.
…Qd7 — Black connects and eyes the light squares.
O-O — king safe; the position becomes chess again.
…h6 — a hedge.
Nc3 — the last minor piece joins.

…Be7 — and Black completes development. The scoreboard reads a third of a pawn for BLACK — the Ponziani's honest price — and his games from here score four in five anyway, because those doubled pawns and the e5 cramp ask questions humans answer worse than engines. Play it knowing both numbers.
playableLines.title: The Bind, Honestly Priced
playableLines.intro: The engine leans Black; his score says White — the doubled pawns and the e5 cramp are why.

title: vs 3…d5 — Qa4 and the great liquidation
overview: The central counter is Black's most principled reply, and the Qa4 pin is the system's answer — 31 of his corpus games reach the junction. From this tabiya the position resolves by liquidation: the pins trade off, the centre pawns trade off, the knights trade off, and what remains is dead level and completely playable. The honest pitch: this line neutralizes Black's best try, and neutral is a fine result against principle.

pieceManeuvers.route: a4 → d1 — the pin's work is done
pieceManeuvers.explanation: When …Bg4 counter-pins, the queen simply returns; the early sortie already forced Black's structure.

strategicThemes: Against the principled reply, equal and simple is a win for the repertoire.
Liquidation is a skill: trade the right pieces in the right order and nothing can go wrong.
The doubled c6-pawns linger after every trade — a small endgame lottery ticket.
endgameTransitions: The final position IS nearly an ending — knight recaptures on e4, structures symmetrical but for Black's doubled c-pawns.

annotations: …Bg4 — Black counter-pins, hitting our e2-bishop through the queen's old square.
Qd1 — so the queen goes home. Its work — the doubled c-pawns Black already carries — is permanent.
…Bxe2 — the light bishops trade.
Qxe2 — recaptured; the queen re-emerges exactly one square better than it started.
…dxe4 — the centre resolves —
dxe4 — pawn for pawn.
…Nxe4 — Black grabs first —

Nxe4 — and we take back. The great liquidation is complete: dead level, symmetrical but for Black's doubled c-pawns, and completely playable. Black's most principled try, met and neutralized — that is what this line is for.
playableLines.title: The Great Liquidation
playableLines.intro: Black plays the principled counter; White trades everything in the right order and stands level with the better pawns.

title: 4…Nxe4 — the dxc6 mayhem, mapped
overview: When Black grabs on e4, dxc6 launches the forcing sequence his corpus rides to a 13-game junction: …Bxf2+ drags our king to e2, the b7-pawn falls, and the queen ends up ON b7 having eaten a bishop. It looks like chaos; it is a map. The engine calls the final reckoning dead level — our king walks but our rook owns g1, Black's f2-knight needs rescuing too. Know the map and the mayhem plays itself; improvise and it eats you.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The queen collects b7 and the bishop behind it — the material that pays for White's walked king.

strategicThemes: Forcing lines are maps, not risks — the danger is only to whoever left the path.
A walked king with the material in hand beats a safe king without it.
Black's f2-knight is as loose as our king — count both sides' problems.
endgameTransitions: Simplification favours whoever untangles first — the g1-rook and f3-knight coordinate faster than Black's scattered pieces.

annotations: …Qf6 — Black centralizes with threats, eyeing our loose kingside.
Na3 — the sleeping knight wakes with a purpose: c4 next, hitting the b6-bishop.
…e4 — the pawn lunges at our f3-knight.
Nc4 — we ignore it one beat longer; the b6-bishop is attacked.
…Rab8 — Black saves the rook from the queen's diagonal, with tempo threats brewing.
Qd5 — the queen re-centralizes from its eating tour, guarding everything at once.
…exf3+ — Black cashes the knight with check —

gxf3 — and the dust settles dead level. Our king has walked, but the g-file rook glares, Black's f2-knight is stranded, and the material ledger balanced itself. The mayhem, mapped — that is the whole trick of the 4…Nxe4 line.
playableLines.title: The Mayhem, Mapped
playableLines.intro: Thirteen corpus games ride this forcing sequence — chaos for the unprepared, a map for us.

title: Rossolimo …g6 — the doubling and the b4 lever
overview: The …g6 Rossolimo did its structural work early: Bxc6 doubled the c-pawns before the fianchetto bishop ever cleared its diagonal. The plan from the tabiya is patient queenside chess — a3 and b4 lever at the front twin, the e3-bishop watches both of them, and Black's e5 stake gives his g7-bishop a permanent pawn in its teeth. Just under half a pawn on the engine, made of structure alone.

pawnBreaks.explanation: a3 prepares it, b4 executes it: the front c-pawn must resolve, and every resolution helps White.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The bishop takes the diagonal where both doubled pawns live and never has to move again.

strategicThemes: Doubled pawns are attacked with levers, not pieces — a3 and b4 do what no knight can.
Black's own …e5 blocks the fianchetto bishop; leave the pawn there and thank it.
Structural edges need no tactics: develop, lever, collect.
endgameTransitions: Every simplification magnifies the c-pawn damage — trade toward the pawn ending without fear.

annotations: …Qc7 — Black connects and watches e5.
a3 — the lever loads quietly.
…a5 — Black tries to stop b4 before it starts.
Be3 — the bishop takes its permanent post, watching both doubled pawns at once.

playableLines.title: The Doubling and the b4 Lever
playableLines.intro: Double them early, lever them late — structure does all the work in the …g6 Rossolimo.

title: Accelerated — the e5 wedge holds the tactics
overview: The positional-squeeze setup: bishops traded on c6, the e5 wedge cramping Black's kingside, b3 and Bb2 supporting it forever. The critical test is tactical — Black throws …c4 and the …Bb4 check trying to shake the wedge loose — and the corpus answer holds through it: block with the knight, absorb the …Qd3 infiltration, and come out just under half a pawn up with the wedge still standing. The squeeze survives its one crisis.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The queen meets Black's d3 infiltration from the corner — ugly for one move, sound forever.

strategicThemes: A wedge is only as good as its worst tactical moment — know this line's and it has none.
Absorb infiltration with the humblest sufficient square.
The e5-cramp fixes Black's kingside knight on g6 for the whole game.
endgameTransitions: If queens trade after the crisis, the e5 wedge and better structure carry every ending.

dxc4 — taken.
…Bb4+ — the check behind the idea.
Nbd2 — blocked with development; nothing bends.
…dxc4 — Black regains the pawn and opens the d-file —
c3 — we put the question to the bishop first.
…Qd3 — the infiltration: the queen lands deep in our camp, the whole point of Black's sequence.

Qb1 — and the humble answer holds everything: the queens must resolve, the e5 wedge still stands, and the engine reads just under half a pawn for White. The squeeze survived its one crisis — that is the entire line, learned.
playableLines.title: The Wedge Holds
playableLines.intro: Black's one tactical crisis against the squeeze — absorbed move by move, wedge intact.

title: Rossolimo …e6 — the queen trade endgame
overview: The …e6 Rossolimo opened the centre on White's terms: the d4 recapture put our queen in the middle of the board with the e1-rook behind it, and Black must spend tempi challenging it. The corpus line's payoff is a trade: when the knight jumps to b4 the queens come off on d8, and the engine grades the resulting ending at six-tenths for White — better development converted directly into a better endgame, no attack required.

pieceManeuvers.explanation: The rook keeps the e-file and covers the second rank against the b4-knight's ideas.
Development completes with the bishop eyeing the queenside Black weakened.

strategicThemes: Development leads convert cleanest through queen trades, not attacks.
An endgame up six-tenths is a bigger edge than a middlegame up six-tenths — fewer ways to lose it.
Black's king on d8 costs three moves to fake castling; charge full price.
endgameTransitions: This line IS the endgame plan — the whole point is arriving there first, king centralized-to-be and rooks connected.

…Kxd8 — castling is gone forever; the king will spend three moves imitating it.
Re2 — the rook stays flexible on the file and covers c2 against the knight.
…Bd7 — Black develops at last.
a3 — the question: the b4-knight has no anchor.
…Nc6 — back it goes; the whole excursion cost Black two tempi.
Be3 — development completes. Six-tenths for White in a queenless position — the development lead converted whole into the endgame, which is exactly this line's business model.
playableLines.title: The Queen Trade Endgame
playableLines.intro: Open the centre first, then charge full price for the queen — six-tenths, queenless, clean.

title: Fantasy main — the Ng5 punishment
overview: The main-line tabiya, and the corpus is unambiguous: five games reached it, five wins. The reason is tactical — with the bishop on c4 and Black's king still deciding, Ng5 doubles on f7, and the natural castling move walks straight into Bxf7+. The engine grades the sequence at +1.7. This plan is less a strategy than a piece of required knowledge: know the punishment, and the main line plays itself.

The most natural move on the board — castling — is the losing one here; that is why this line must be KNOWN.
Convert tactics into material, then let the material talk.
endgameTransitions: Up the exchange, every trade is a step toward a won rook ending.

title: Fantasy …e6 — Ne2, long castle, the a3 question
overview: The solid …e6 line — 19 corpus games, 14 wins. Opposite-side castling turns a quiet French wall into a race.

title: Fantasy …g6 — the Ng4 poke and the d5 counter
overview: The fianchetto line is Black's best try against the Fantasy — 16 corpus games, 11 wins, and the engine puts this continuation a hair below level. That honesty is the plan: know that …Ng4 pokes at the e3-bishop, tuck it to g1 rather than concede it, and when Black stakes the centre with …e5, push THROUGH with d5 and collect on c6. A hair below level with ideas beats half a pawn up without them.

…e5 — Black stakes the centre, striking at d4.

…Nf6 — the g4-knight walks back to hit our d5-pawn — the poke gained nothing.

Be3 — and the bishop returns to the post it never really left. A hair below level on the engine — this is Black's best line against the Fantasy, and both sides have their share of the play. Honest chess.

title: The h-file storm — crash through on h2 (Accepted main line)
overview: Out of the accepted main line, this is the plan that defines this repertoire's Stafford: with the queen, knight and bishop already trained on f2, Black throws the h-pawn forward to h4, blows open the h-file, and the rook on h8 crashes into White's king. We are a pawn down and we do not care — the king is the target. This is the structure this repertoire used to mate a grandmaster at the 2024 World Blitz, and it follows his win over FarewellToKings (2661).

title: Four Knights — trade the c4-bishop, play on the doubled pawns
overview: The 3.Nc3 Four Knights is this repertoire's highest-scoring branch (68%), and it is positional, not a mating attack — so we teach it honestly. After White trades the dark bishops and doubles its own e-pawns, Black challenges the strong light-squared bishop with …Na5 and …Nxb3, plays …c6 to build a small centre, and lifts the queen to b6 to pressure the queenside and the backward b-pawn. title: Glek System: Ne2, f4 and the Bishop Trap
overview: The Glek's quiet fianchetto hides real venom. If Black castles too early instead of the mandatory ...d6, the centre fork trick — Nxe5, then d4 — hands White the bishop pair and dark-square control; and if Black then commits ...d6, the dark-squared bishop marooned on e5 becomes a target. The winning idea is prophylaxis first: step the knight off c3 with Ne2 so f4 no longer runs into ...Bxc3, and only THEN unleash f4, g4 and the Nc3-e2-g3-f5 march. Black's bishop is trapped or entombed and White's 'boring' setup becomes a raging kingside attack.

g4 grabs space, clamps f5, and threatens g5 to shove the bishop further back. Behind the g2-bishop, White's king is safe enough to storm.

playableLines.title: The Bishop Trap and the Kingside Storm
playableLines.intro: Black has just played ...d6, blocking the e5-bishop's retreat. White punishes it with prophylaxis and a pawn storm.
annotations: The prophylactic masterstroke. It looks like a meek retreat, but Knight to e2 is the entire point of the position. White resists the natural f4 for one move — because with the knight still on c3, Black would meet f4 with Bxc3, shattering White's pawns and swarming the e4-pawn. Step off c3 first: now there is nothing to capture, e4 is granite, and the knight sets off — first to g3, then onward to the dream square f5.

Black is already worse and must find the only move. With f4 coming to hit the e5-bishop — its retreat to d6 walled off by Black's own pawn — the knight drops sadly back to d7 just to open the f6-escape for the bishop. A developing piece un-develops purely to keep a bishop breathing.

Now it lands. The pawn jabs the bishop on e5 and there is no knight on c3 to snatch anymore. White's centre stays rock-solid, the f-file cracks open for the rook, and a broad pawn front rolls forward — one move that harasses a piece AND launches the attack.
The bishop trudges to f6, the single square Black's last move unlocked. Alive, but buried — a big piece turned spectator behind its own pawns while White's initiative gathers speed.

The storm breaks. g4 seizes kingside space, nails down the f5-square, and readies g5 to boot the f6-bishop back even further. Tucked behind the g2-bishop, White's king is snug, so the pawns charge with a clear conscience.
Black throws up a barricade to contest f5 and give the king a breath of air. But loosening the kingside in front of the g2-bishop and the rolling pawns only gifts White fresh targets.

The knight completes its long march — c3 to e2 to g3 — and glares at f5, the eternal outpost where a knight sits beyond the reach of pawns and rules the board. Braced by the g4-pawn and the g2-bishop, it is the crown jewel of White's whole setup.

Black buries the bishop on g7, entombed behind the g6- and f7-pawns. Survey the wreckage: White commands a rolling pawn storm, the f5 outpost, open lines for both rooks, and a g2-bishop that towers over its wretched rival. From a 'boring' fianchetto, White has built a near-winning kingside bind — the Glek's hidden venom, laid bare.

title: Sämisch queenside play — a4, Nb5, open the a-file
overview: In the Sämisch King's Indian your big pawn centre lets you open a second front. a4 gains space and Nb5 pokes at c7 and d6; when Black takes the knight, axb5 opens the a-file for your rook. You play on the wing where you are strong while Black's kingside counterplay is slow.

title: The classical centre — d4-e4 and the long diagonal
overview: The Exchange Grünfeld is the great centre-versus-piece-pressure battle. You build the d4-e4 pawn mass and, in the sharpest line, meet Black's …Bxa1 by recapturing with the queen — the monarch rakes the long diagonal while your central pawns roll. Engine-equal, dynamically rich, and exactly the fight the variation is about.

title: Nimzo Qc2 — the bishop pair and the central files
overview: The whole point of 4.Qc2 is to recapture on c3 with the queen and keep the bishop pair with no doubled pawns. Now you convert that structural asset: Rd1 and Rc1 grip the central files, Ne2 and Bf2 regroup behind the pawns, and you sit on a small, durable pull with the two bishops.

title: Fight for e4 — the central knight and the wedge
overview: The Queen's Indian is a battle for the e4-square. You plant a knight on e5, and after the trade dxe5 builds a central wedge that cramps Black; Bxe4 then collects the light-squared prize the fianchetto was meant to guard. Small, clean edge on the squares Black's whole setup was built to control.

title: Staunton Gambit — lead in development for the pawn
overview: The Staunton Gambit trades a pawn for a lead in development against the Dutch. You keep the initiative simple: castle, swing the queen to f4 and the bishop to h4 to press the dark squares and pin Black's pieces. When the smoke clears you have activity and easy play worth every bit of the pawn.

title: Exchange QGD — restrain, then grind the centre
overview: The Exchange QGD gives you the classic minority-attack structure, but the flexible modern handling is to first restrain Black's counterplay. a4 stops …b5 and …a5, Qc2 and the rooks pile behind the centre, and you keep every option — minority attack or central e-file play — while Black has none.

control of the centre

title: Refuse the Budapest — keep the space, expand a4-b4
overview: Return the Budapest pawn on your terms and keep a lasting space edge. With the centre stable, a4 and b4 roll on the queenside, gaining room and squares while Black's gambit pieces have nothing to bite on. Simple, strong, and exactly how to neutralise a tricky gambit — take the space and play chess.

title: Neutralise the London — trade the pieces, reach equality
overview: The London System wants a cosy attacking setup; you defuse it by trading. Meet the e5-knight and later the d3-bishop with clean exchanges — every swap kills a piece of White's attack. When the dust settles you have a sound, symmetrical position and full equality, exactly what Black is after against a system opening.

the solid pawn structure
endgameTransitions: simplify into a comfortable, level endgame

overview: Against the Catalan the freeing break is …e5. Once your pieces are ready, …e5 challenges White's centre, opens lines for your bishops and unshackles the position Black's setup can feel cramped in. The engine calls it dead equal — and the initiative that comes with a well-timed central break is worth more than the number suggests.

title: Plant the knight on e4
overview: The Colle is a quiet system, and the cleanest antidote is a piece on e4. You double rooks on the central files and drop a knight into e4 — a permanent outpost in the heart of White's cramped setup. From that square the knight radiates, and Black takes over the initiative in an equal but easier-to-play position.

overview: The Smith-Morra hands you a pawn for development; the sound path is to take it, return it if needed, and complete development safely. overview: Against the c3 Alapin, sound development neutralises White's centre. White's small space edge means nothing when every file is covered and every piece is ideally placed.

overview: The classical antidote to the King's Gambit is to hold the extra pawn and develop. Here it goes further: …Nxd4 and …Qxd4+ win a second pawn and, after the king steps aside, …Qxb2 harvests a third while raking White's queenside. Two pawns up with a sound position, Black is simply better — the gambit refuted.
